# Getting started

I review and verify the latest merged PRs for your project. I read the code, run checks, test real user flows and read the deploy logs, then give a PASS, FAIL or INCOMPLETE verdict with the evidence.

Ask these one at a time, and wait for each answer:
1. What should I call you, and what's your timezone?
2. Which repo should I watch, and what's your GitHub login? Check that `gh` is signed in as you.
3. How do your branches map to environments (dev, staging, production), and where is it hosted? Offer to connect Railway if that's the host.
4. Which issue tracker do you use? If it's Linear and you have more than one workspace, which repos belong to which?
5. Which user flows matter most, and which test accounts am I allowed to use?
6. Do you want a weekday morning list of your issues and tickets to work on? If so, what time?

Then save the answers as memories, connect the services they named, and create the morning routine if they said yes.

# GitHub issue reply when the fix is merged

The repo is `MystenLabs/MemWal`. Write in American English. When this skill runs, post the comment; don't leave it as a draft.

Source: [walrus-memory-github-issue-reply-templates](https://docs.google.com/document/d/182NqV2Nf4nITJrsEdyfB_E7KnNPredZll-dWj7giHL4/edit). This skill covers only the merged-fix reply.

## When

Use it when the fix PR is **merged** and Henry or Hari (whoever asked) wants the issue comment posted.

If the fix isn't merged yet, post this instead, with the real PR URL:

```
Thanks for the detailed report. We reproduced this on <version / environment> and confirmed the root cause is <one-line cause>. A fix is in progress and tracked in <PR url>; we will update this thread when it ships.
```

## When not to use this template

Skip it for a vulnerability, or for a security, data-integrity or availability report that isn't safe to discuss in public:

- Post no template reply, and add no extra detail on the issue.
- Security routes critical items to Thanos Bourgos or Yannis.
- If there's a public holding note, it's one line with no detail, and it comes from Thanos or Yannis.

A data-loss or downtime bug that is safe to discuss in public still gets the reply below.

## Comment

Fill every bracket from the PR and leave none in the posted text. Don't invent a version.

```
Thanks for flagging this. We reproduced it, and the fix is merged in <PR url> and will be included in <release>. Please reopen if you still see it after upgrading.
```

That sentence is the whole reply. It thanks the reporter, says we reproduced the bug and merged the fix, names the release, and invites a reopen after upgrading. Don't add "not true", "invalid", "wrong" or a bare "closing".

```bash
gh issue comment <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal --body-file <file>
```

If the GitHub issue is still `OPEN` after the PR is merged into `dev` (for example, when merging into `dev` instead of `main`, or when a single PR fixes multiple issues), **close the GitHub issue** right after posting the comment:

```bash
gh issue close <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal
```

## Parallel Post-Merge Workflow (`gh-issue-fixed` + `walm-ticket` + `memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet`)

Whenever a PR that solves a GitHub issue has **100% CI checks GREEN (`SUCCESS`)** and **`APPROVED`** review and is merged into `dev`, execute these three steps in parallel:
1. **`gh-issue-fixed` (GitHub Issue)**: Post the merged-fix comment above on every GitHub issue solved by the PR and ensure the issue is **CLOSED** (`gh issue close <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal` if still `OPEN`).
2. **`walm-ticket` (Linear `linear-mysten`)**: Move the corresponding `WALM-*` ticket(s) to **`Done`** and post a comment linking the merged PR URL, merge commit SHA, release version, and closed GitHub issue(s).
3. **`memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet` (`dev` Verification)**: Verify the `dev` deployment (`https://relayer.dev.memwal.ai/version`, `/health`, Railway `dev` logs, and `memwal-dev-wallet` E2E check) to confirm the merged changes run cleanly on `dev`.

## Retired Standalone Demo Apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`)

The standalone demo apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`) are **disabled and no longer maintained** (note: `apps/app`, the core Dashboard / Playground web console, remains actively maintained).

- **Do not** open or merge PRs targeting `apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, or `apps/researcher`.
- If an open PR targets one of these retired demo apps, close the PR (`gh pr close <PR> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal --comment "..."`) explaining that the demo app is retired and no longer maintained.
- If an open GitHub issue targets `apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, or `apps/researcher`, post this reply and close the issue as `not planned`:

```
Thanks for reporting this. The standalone demo apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, and `apps/researcher`) have been retired and are no longer maintained as we focus on the core Walrus Memory relayer, SDKs, MCP server, OpenClaw plugin, and Dashboard (`apps/app`). Closing this issue as not planned.
```

```bash
gh issue comment <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal --body-file <file>
gh issue close <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal --reason "not planned"
```

- Also move the corresponding Linear `WALM-*` ticket (if any) to **`Canceled`** via `walm-ticket`.

## Before posting

- Make sure `gh auth status` shows the requester's own account (verify with `gh auth status`).
- **Never include internal `WALM-*` Linear ticket IDs** in the GitHub issue comment (keep `WALM-*` strictly inside Linear `linear-mysten`, and update the corresponding `WALM-*` ticket to `Done` or `Canceled` on Linear).
- **Verify real reproduction and 100% green CI**: Confirm the issue was genuinely reproduced end-to-end (`Local vs dev` / live `dev` or integration test) and the fixing PR merged with 100% green CI and deploy checks (`dev` and `production` are the only active environments; `staging` is retired).
- Check that the PR link points to the merged PR.
- Make sure `<release>` is the version the fix ships in, from the changelog or the version bump on the PR. If you don't know it, ask whoever requested the reply. Don't guess, and don't write "the next release" unless that's true.
- Post one comment, close the issue if still `OPEN`, and don't edit the issue body.

# Linear org routing

Use this whenever Linear work could touch more than one workspace (e.g. Mysten Labs vs CommandOSS). Linear MCP is one org per auth session, so this bot keeps separate servers and picks by path.

## Before any Linear tool call

1. Resolve the **working directory** for the task:
   - Prefer the path on the user's machine for the repo/folder they named or have open.
   - If they only named a project (MemWal, Prydea, …), map it through `registry.yaml` in this skill folder.
2. Read `registry.yaml` beside this skill (same folder as `SKILL.md`).
3. Match the path (or project name) against `path_patterns` / `name_patterns` **in order**. First match wins.
4. Use only the matched entry's `mcp_server` name for Linear tools. Never call a different Linear server for that task.
5. If nothing matches:
   - Ask which org (Mysten Labs / CommandOSS), or
   - Use `default_mcp_server` only when the user explicitly says the default is fine.
6. Say the choice briefly once ("using `linear-mysten` for this MemWal path") then proceed.

## Registry shape

```yaml
default_mcp_server: null
orgs:
  - id: mysten
    label: Mysten Labs
    mcp_server: linear-mysten
    path_patterns: [...]
    name_patterns: [...]
```

`mcp_server` must match the installed MCP server name exactly (`linear-mysten`, `linear-commandoss`).

## Editing the registry

When the user adds a repo or folder to an org, update `registry.yaml` only — do not hard-code paths into this recipe.

## MCP setup notes (for humans / install)

Two stdio servers, same Linear endpoint, **separate** auth dirs:

```text
linear-mysten:      MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR=<auth-dir>/mysten-labs
linear-commandoss:  MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR=<auth-dir>/commandoss
command: npx
args: ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"]
```

Authenticate each server once (pick the right Linear org in the OAuth flow). Do not reuse one auth dir for both.

# QA MemWal (Per-Item Acceptance & Verification)

Acts as Hari's QA on MemWal (`MystenLabs/MemWal`) and the Railway project **Walrus Memory** (id `7c541ac5-535d-4240-9bad-4ad9804c2dd7`): runs the acceptance checklist for each handed-off item and says PASS or FAIL before he ships.

## Workflow for every item (PR, Linear WALM ticket, or fix)

1. **Scope**:
   - Identify the environment from the branch (`dev` → `dev`, `main` → `production` only after confirming the deploy mapping; note: `staging` is retired and no longer used — promotions go directly `dev → main`).
   - Check whether the PR's head or merge commit is deployed on Railway **Walrus Memory** (`curl -s <relayer>/version | jq .build.commit` and `railway status --json`).

2. **Build the acceptance checklist**:
   - Derive from the PR diff, the ticket's acceptance criteria, and affected user flows:
     - Relayer API
     - SDK (TypeScript / Python)
     - MCP (`init`, `tools`, `auth`, `remember`, job polling to terminal state, `recall`, reconnect)
     - Playground
     - Demo apps (`chatbot`, `noter`, `researcher`)
   - Include one regression check per indirectly affected consumer.

3. **Run it for real**:
   - Run automated tests, type checks, and builds, plus real user flows.
   - **If the PR is deployed**: test the live env.
   - **If the PR is NOT deployed**: don't stop at `PENDING` — check out the PR head in a private clone/worktree, pull the `dev` env config from Railway (read-only, e.g. `list-variables` for the `dev` env; keep values in local env files only, never print or commit them), run the relayer/sidecar/MCP/apps locally against `dev`'s backing services with authorized test accounts, and run the full checklist there. Label these results **`Local vs dev`** and keep the live deployed checks `PENDING` until it ships.
   - Follow every write to its terminal state and recall the content with a unique marker. A `202` or a green `/health` is not a pass.
   - Use a real browser for UI flows.

4. **Check Railway logs**:
   - When something is deployed, check Railway logs for the deploy window: crashes, restarts, 5xx, timeouts, stuck jobs, signer errors.

5. **Report**:
   - Start with: `[Env]: PASS / FAIL / INCOMPLETE, one sentence`
   - Provide:
     - Checklist table (`Check` | `Result` | `Evidence` | `Where it ran: Local vs dev or Live`)
     - Timings (mark unmeasured timings as `unmeasured`)
     - Suggested review comments
     - Missing tests
     - What was skipped and why

## Hard Rules

- Never deploy, merge, run migrations, change shared config or Railway variables, open tickets, or message anyone.
- Local runs must not mutate shared `dev` state beyond test-account writes.
- Before any live or `Local vs dev` burst, check no other task is deploying or benchmarking the same env.
- Use an isolated worktree/clone, not a dirty shared checkout.
- Redact all secrets.
- A sidecar `503` is not proof of an upstream `429`.
- Never claim `PASS` from code review or mocks alone. Read the entire issue/PR thread, reproduce the bug on the base branch, and verify the fix end-to-end.
- **All-Green CI & Deploy Gate**: Never report a PR as merge-ready (`PASS` to merge) if ANY GitHub Actions check or Railway/Vercel deployment check on the PR head (`statusCheckRollup`, `check-runs`, or commit `status`) is `FAILURE`, `ERROR`, `CANCELLED`, `IN_PROGRESS`, or `PENDING`, or if the target branch (`dev` or `main`) has a failing CI or broken/cancelled Railway deploy.
- **Retired Standalone Demo Apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`)**: Standalone demo apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`) are disabled and no longer maintained (only `apps/app`, the core Dashboard / Playground web console, remains actively maintained). Do not merge PRs for those demo apps; close their PRs and close related GitHub issues as `not planned` (moving Linear `WALM-*` tickets to `Canceled`).
- Verify your active GitHub account via `gh auth status` before pushing, commenting, or reviewing.
- Reply casually and briefly in English, times in ICT (`UTC+7`).

name: memwal-review
description: >-

  environment (dev or production) with code review, automated checks,
  real user-flow tests and Railway logs, and end with a PASS / FAIL /

  merged PRs, verify a deploy, or decide if dev → main is safe (staging is

# MemWal environment review (reviewer)

Review and verify the latest merged PRs for MemWal through code review, relevant automated checks, real user-flow tests, and Railway logs.

Use the current conversation's incidents, reported identifiers, and previous findings as investigation leads. Re-check their current status rather than assuming earlier conclusions still hold.

Optional overrides (ask only if the request is ambiguous):
- Target environment: infer from the current branch if blank
- PRs or time range: infer from deployment history if blank
- Specific incident or flow: optional

Fixed facts:
- Repo `MystenLabs/MemWal` (`MystenLabs/walrus-memory`); Railway project **Walrus Memory** (id `7c541ac5-535d-4240-9bad-4ad9804c2dd7`) with **dev** and **production** environments (`staging` is retired and no longer used; promotions go directly `dev → main`).
- Relayers: dev `https://relayer.dev.memwal.ai`, prod `https://relayer.memory.walrus.xyz`. `curl -s <relayer>/version | jq .build.commit` gives the deployed commit.
- Deploy targets are NOT guaranteed to be the namesake branches (see 2026-09-28 drift). Always place `build.commit` in git (`git branch -r --contains <sha>`) before claiming anything about an environment.
- GitHub account is `harrymove-ctrl` (`harrymove-ctrl <harry.phan@commandoss.com>`); check `gh auth status` first. If `gh` reports an x509 / invalid-token error inside the sandbox, use `curl` with `gh auth token`.
- Tickets: WALM team on `linear-mysten` (see `linear-org-routing` and `walm-ticket`).

## 1. Establish scope

Read repository instructions and identify the current branch.

Default environment:
- dev → dev only.
- main/production → production only after confirming the actual deployment mapping.
- (`staging` is retired — do not target or test `staging`).
- Feature branch → determine its intended base and test environment; never assume production.

For a promotion:
- Before deployment, review the promotion diff and relevant source-environment evidence.
- After deployment, validate the destination environment.
- Do not claim destination validation from source-environment results.

Do not test every environment by default. Expand only when requested or necessary to investigate a specific dependency, and explain why.

State the selected environment, change range, and intended coverage before testing.

## 2. Determine what changed and what is actually deployed

- Fetch the latest relevant branches.
- Inspect merged PRs and actual diffs, including changes hidden inside broadly titled PRs.
- Identify deployed commits for every relevant service.
- Compare against the previous deployment or requested baseline.
- Audit every merged PR's `statusCheckRollup` and its merge commit's `check-runs` + commit `status` (including Railway `Walrus Memory - *` deployment statuses): flag any PR that was merged while a CI job or Playwright E2E check was `FAILURE`, `CANCELLED`, or still `IN_PROGRESS`, or where a Railway service deployment errored/cancelled. Never recommend promotion or merge unless 100% of CI checks and Railway deploy checks are completed and `SUCCESS` (`GREEN`).
- Separate: merged into the branch; present in the deployed artifact; verified through live testing.
- Check migrations, dependency versions, configuration requirements, and compatibility across services, SDKs, MCP, and apps.
- Map changes to affected user flows and indirect consumers.
- If changes are merged but not deployed, perform local checks and mark live validation pending. Do not deploy automatically.

## 3. Run meaningful tests

- Run relevant automated tests, type checks, and builds.
- Use authorized test accounts for deployed tests.
- Confirm every app/client points to the selected environment and network.
- Exercise affected MCP flows: initialization, tool discovery, auth, remember, job-status polling, recall, and reconnect.
- Exercise account creation/lookup, delegate auth, and identity-link prerequisites where relevant.
- Test the playground and affected demo apps, including chatbot, noter, researcher, and other apps found in the repository.
- Use real browser interactions for affected UI flows.
- For shared backend, SDK, auth, contract, or deployment changes, test affected consumers even when their own code did not change.
- Scale test depth to impact. Do not run every app's full suite for unrelated changes.
- Explain skipped checks and distinguish irrelevant checks from blocked ones.

## 4. Verify writes and timing end to end

- A 202, job_id, successful build, or green /health does not prove the user flow works.
- Follow a test write to its terminal state, confirm completion, and recall the expected content.
- Check that failures surface useful errors and exhausted retries do not remain running.
- Verify indexer progress and account visibility against known on-chain state when relevant.
- Measure acceptance, preparation, upload/completion, polling, recall, and affected UI/MCP latency separately where observable.
- Investigate unexpected latency and timeout behavior. Do not increase timeouts merely to make tests pass.
- Use unique test markers and isolated test data.
- Clean up only data created by this run, where supported.
- Use local or isolated tests for fault injection; do not deliberately disrupt shared services.

## 5. Inspect Railway logs across the selected environment

- Confirm the Railway project, environment, services, and deployed commits (`railway status --json`; walk `environments.edges[].node.serviceInstances.edges[].node.{serviceName, latestDeployment.meta.{branch,commitHash}}`).
- Inspect every service in that environment for failure signals, then investigate affected services and dependencies in depth.
- Include relayer, indexer, sidecar/MCP, workers, demo apps, and supporting services hosted on Railway. Identify components sharing a deployment.
- Review deployment, build, startup, runtime, and HTTP logs where available.
- Cover the relevant deployment-to-present window and a comparable pre-deployment baseline where retention allows.
- Use filtering, pagination, and time windows. Do not rely only on the last few log lines.
- Look for crashes, restarts, OOMs, migration errors, connection failures, unexpected 4xx/5xx, slow requests, timeouts, repeated retries, queue backlogs, stuck jobs, and checkpoint decoding failures.
- Correlate events across services and live tests using timestamps, request IDs, job IDs, account IDs, and transaction digests.
- Check available metrics for resource pressure, queue growth, indexer lag, and latency changes.
- Distinguish new regressions, pre-existing issues, and expected negative-test errors.
- For significant findings, capture frequency, first/last occurrence, representative redacted logs, and user impact.
- State log retention gaps, unavailable sources, and sampling limitations.
- Check whether health/readiness reporting reflects actual behavior.

## 6. Trace failures and check existing fixes

For each failure:
- Identify the failing component separately from the app or team experiencing the symptom.
- Trace the sequence from request acceptance to the failing operation.
- Distinguish confirmed cause from a hypothesis.
- Search the latest relevant branches and merged PRs for an existing fix before proposing new work.
- Inspect the implementation, not just PR titles or descriptions.
- Report whether the fix is: not implemented; open in a PR; merged but not deployed; deployed but not verified; verified in the selected environment.
- Link the relevant PR and commit.
- Do not suggest reimplementing a fix already merged.
- Do not call an issue resolved merely because a fix exists in code.

## 7. Execution boundaries

- Take the time needed to complete meaningful verification. Stop repeating checks once sufficient evidence exists.
- Use approved credentials without exposing secrets.
- Preserve unrelated local changes.
- Do not deploy, merge, run migrations, change shared configuration, or apply fixes during this review.
- Limit live mutations to isolated authorized test activity.
- Complete independent checks before asking for missing access or approval.
- Do not create tickets or send messages unless requested.
- Do not claim live success based on code inspection, mocks, or tests against another commit or environment.

## 8. Communicate clearly throughout

- Give concise progress updates with findings, uncertainty, and the next check.
- Lead with the practical result, not a chronological tool transcript.
- Explain technical errors in plain language and connect them to user impact.
- Clearly name which component failed; do not blame the consuming app without evidence.
- Use exact error text, timestamps with timezone, and identifiers only where they help substantiate the finding.
- Correct earlier conclusions explicitly when new evidence changes them.
- Match the user's language. Keep team-message drafts in concise, natural English unless requested otherwise.

## Final response

Start with:
"[Environment]: PASS / FAIL / INCOMPLETE — [one-sentence conclusion]."

Then provide:

**A. Scope**
- Branch, reviewed baseline, deployed service commits, and PRs covered.
- Changes merged but not yet deployed.

**B. Findings** — compact table:
Issue / Failing component / Evidence and user impact / Existing fix or PR / Deployment and verification status

**C. Tests** — compact table:
Flow / Environment and tested commit / Result / Timing / Evidence

**D. Railway review**
- Significant findings and affected services.
- Coverage window, unavailable logs, and remaining gaps.

**E. Next steps**
- Concrete actions in priority order.
- Separate new implementation from deploying existing fixes and completing validation.
- State whether promotion is recommended, or whether the deployed promotion is verified.
- If a known incident is involved, include a short ready-to-send update explaining what happened, what is already fixed, and what remains. Draft only; do not send.

Verdict rules:
- FAIL: a relevant failure is confirmed. Also disclose any incomplete checks.
- INCOMPLETE: essential validation is missing and no confirmed failure already determines the verdict.
- PASS: relevant checks passed against the intended deployed commits, with explicit coverage limits.
- Never imply other environments were verified or guarantee that no bugs exist.

## 9. Parallel Post-Merge Reconciliation (`memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet` + `gh-issue-fixed` + `walm-ticket`)

Whenever an `APPROVED` + `100% CI GREEN` PR that solves a GitHub issue is merged into `dev`, run these three workflows in parallel:
1. **`memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet` (`dev` Verification)**: Verify the newly deployed `dev` commit on `https://relayer.dev.memwal.ai/version` and `/health`, inspect Railway `dev` logs and release workflow runs (`Release SDK`, `Release Python SDK`, `Release Walrus Memory OpenClaw Plugin`), and execute a `memwal-dev-wallet` / SDK end-to-end runtime check against `dev`.
2. **`gh-issue-fixed` (GitHub Issue Reply & Close)**: Post the standard merged-fix comment on every GitHub issue solved by the PR (naming the PR URL and release version, without any `WALM-*` IDs) and close the GitHub issue (`gh issue close <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal` if it is still `OPEN`).
3. **`walm-ticket` (Linear `linear-mysten`)**: Update the corresponding `WALM-*` ticket(s) to **`Done`** and post a comment linking the merged PR URL, merge commit SHA, release version, and closed GitHub issue(s).

## 10. Retired Standalone Demo Apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`)

- The standalone demo applications (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`) are **disabled and no longer maintained** (note: `apps/app`, the core Dashboard / Playground web console, remains actively maintained).
- Do not implement fixes or merge PRs targeting `apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, or `apps/researcher`. Close open PRs targeting those demo apps, close their GitHub issues (`--reason "not planned"`) with a note that the demo apps are retired and no longer maintained, and move corresponding Linear `WALM-*` tickets to **`Canceled`**.

# MemWal Skill Hub & Team Rule Sync (`memwal-mcp` + `walrus-console-mcp`)

Use this skill whenever a team member wants to:
1. **Fetch / pull shared skills (`SKILL.md`)** and their active **Team Rules** from a shared Walrus namespace (such as `memwal-team-skills` or `design-skills`) into `~/.agents/skills/` and `~/.gemini/config/skills/`.
2. **Host / push a new or updated `SKILL.md`** revision into the shared Walrus Console bucket (`skills-<ns>`) and publish a `[SKILL_REF:<id>]` pointer so teammates can pull it.
3. **Teach a Skill (Add / Toggle / Bake Team Rule)**: Record a newly discovered rule (`[RULE:<ruleId>]`) or state transition (`[RULE_STATE:<ruleId>]`) so every teammate's coding agent folds the latest active rules deterministically.

## 1. Memory & Console Tagging Contract inside a Namespace Folder

A Walrus `namespace` acts as a shared **Skill Folder** (for example, `memwal-team-skills`). Every entry uses one of four structured records:

1. **Skill Revision Pointer (`[SKILL_REF:<skill-name>]`)**:
   ```json
   [SKILL_REF:memwal-qa]
   {"id":"memwal-qa","bucketId":"bucket-memwal-team-skills","fileId":"console-file-memwal-qa-r2","sha256":"...","rev":2,"updatedAt":"2026-11-02T12:00:00Z","author":"@harrymove-ctrl"}
   ```

   When `walrus-console-mcp` (`console_download_file`) is configured, download `<skill-name>.SKILL.md` by `fileId`. Otherwise fall back to the newest `[SKILL:<skill-name>]` memory payload.

1. Fold all `[RULE:<ruleId>]`, `[RULE_STATE:<ruleId>]`, and legacy `[FLOW:<skill-name>]` events in chronological order (or newest-first by `rev` and `updatedAt`).

3. Append only active (`state === "on"`) rules to the bottom of the local `~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` under `## Learned Team Rules (Synced from Walrus)`.

# MCP & Linear Workspace Routing Skill

Use this skill whenever an agent needs to access MCP servers or Linear issue tracking tools, ensuring operations route to the correct workspace and team based on the active project directory path.

## When to Use

- Before calling any Linear MCP tool (`list_issues`, `save_issue`, `get_team`, `list_teams`, etc.).
- When working across multi-project environments (`commandoss` vs `mysten-lab`).
- When determining which tracker workspace and team overview URL applies to the current session.

## Core Rules

1. **Path-to-Workspace Association**:
   - `/Users/synasapmob/Documents/commandoss/*` or `*Prydea*` or `*commandoss*`:
     - Linear Workspace: `https://linear.app/commandoss`
     - Team: `PRDEA`
     - Team Overview: `https://linear.app/commandoss/team/PRDEA/overview`
     - Auth Config: `~/.mcp-auth/commandoss`
   - `/Users/synasapmob/Documents/mysten-lab/*` or `*mysten*` or `*walrus*` or `*sui*`:
     - Linear Workspace: `https://linear.app/mysten-labs`
     - Team: `WALM`
     - Auth Config: `~/.mcp-auth/mysten-labs`
   - Any project with `linear.status: disabled` (e.g. `githubRepo/helloWorld`):
     - Never make Linear MCP calls.

2. **Step-by-Step Procedure**:
   - **Step 1**: Check the current working directory (`pwd` or workspace context).
   - **Step 2**: Inspect `registry.yaml` (workspace root or `~/.gemini/config/registry.yaml`).
   - **Step 3**: Identify the project matching the current path.
   - **Step 4**: Verify the configured Linear workspace. If working on Prydea, ensure you are interacting with team `PRDEA` in `commandoss` (`https://linear.app/commandoss/team/PRDEA/overview`).
   - **Step 5**: If the active MCP session is connected to a different workspace (e.g. `mysten-labs` when in Prydea), isolate session tokens via `MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.mcp-auth/commandoss` or prompt the user for the corresponding workspace re-authentication.

# Rust Async Patterns

Production patterns for async Rust programming with Tokio runtime, including tasks, channels, streams, and error handling.

## When to Use This Skill

- Building async Rust applications
- Implementing concurrent network services
- Using Tokio for async I/O
- Handling async errors properly
- Debugging async code issues
- Optimizing async performance

## Core Concepts

### 1. Async Execution Model

```
Future (lazy) → poll() → Ready(value) | Pending
                ↑           ↓
              Waker ← Runtime schedules
```

### 2. Key Abstractions

| Concept    | Purpose                                  |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `Future`   | Lazy computation that may complete later |
| `async fn` | Function returning impl Future           |
| `await`    | Suspend until future completes           |
| `Task`     | Spawned future running concurrently      |
| `Runtime`  | Executor that polls futures              |

## Quick Start

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
futures = "0.3"
async-trait = "0.1"
anyhow = "1.0"
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = "0.3"
```

```rust
use tokio::time::{sleep, Duration};
use anyhow::Result;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    // Initialize tracing
    tracing_subscriber::fmt::init();

    // Async operations
    let result = fetch_data("https://api.example.com").await?;
    println!("Got: {}", result);

    Ok(())
}

async fn fetch_data(url: &str) -> Result<String> {
    // Simulated async operation
    sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
    Ok(format!("Data from {}", url))
}
```

## Detailed patterns and worked examples

Detailed pattern documentation lives in `references/details.md`. Read that file when the navigation tier above is insufficient.

## Best Practices

### Do's

- **Use `tokio::select!`** - For racing futures
- **Prefer channels** - Over shared state when possible
- **Use `JoinSet`** - For managing multiple tasks
- **Instrument with tracing** - For debugging async code
- **Handle cancellation** - Check `CancellationToken`

### Don'ts

- **Don't block** - Never use `std::thread::sleep` in async
- **Don't hold locks across awaits** - Causes deadlocks
- **Don't spawn unboundedly** - Use semaphores for limits
- **Don't ignore errors** - Propagate with `?` or log
- **Don't forget Send bounds** - For spawned futures

name: rust-best-practices
description: >-
  Write idiomatic, robust, maintainable Rust. Use this skill whenever you write, review,
  refactor, debug, or explain Rust code: new crates, modules, functions, structs, traits,

  any mention of Rust, cargo, crates, .rs files, the borrow checker, lifetimes, traits,
  clippy, or rustfmt, even when the user does not ask for "best practices" or "idiomatic"
  code. Synthesized from the Google Rust Style Guide, the Rust API Guidelines,
  Effective Rust, Rust Design Patterns, and Microsoft's Pragmatic Rust Guidelines.
---

# Rust best practices

Distilled from five Rust style and design guides, with a digest of each in `references/`.
Where they disagree, this file says which to follow and why.

## 1. Mindset

- **Write Rust-shaped code.** Don't port C++, Java, C#, or Python constructs one-to-one.
  Model errors with `Result`, resources with ownership and `Drop`, polymorphism with
  traits and enums, and nullability with `Option`. Inheritance-flavored tricks (`Deref` to
  a "base" struct, `Manager`/`Factory` types, `throw_if_null` helpers) are smells.
- **Make invalid states unrepresentable.** Push invariants into types: enums instead of
  bool flags and "must be X if Y" comments, newtypes for units and IDs, fallible
  constructors that validate once. The compiler then enforces what a comment could only
  request.
- **Application code is not library code.** Library code (anything with external users)
  follows the API-design rules below strictly. Application code should favor simplicity
  and directness: concrete types, `anyhow`-style errors, `Vec` return values, no
  speculative generality.
- **Let the tools do the work.** rustfmt owns formatting, clippy owns idiom checks, the
  compiler owns memory safety. Spend your attention on design.

## 2. Before you hand back code

Run these and fix everything they report:

```bash
cargo fmt
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
cargo doc --no-deps   # libraries: catches broken doc links and missing docs
```

- Fix a lint rather than silencing it. When a lint is genuinely wrong for one item, use
  `#[expect(clippy::name, reason = "...")]` on the narrowest item. `expect` warns when
  the lint stops firing, so stale suppressions get cleaned up. Use `#[allow]` only in
  generated code or macro output.
- Never put `#![deny(warnings)]` in source: new toolchains add warnings and break the
  build. Enforce warnings-as-errors in CI instead, with `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`.
- Configure lints once in `Cargo.toml` (`[lints]` or `[workspace.lints]`), not with
  scattered crate attributes. If a project has none, suggest `lints/lints.toml` and
  `lints/clippy.toml` from https://github.com/morganlinton/BeautifulRust; the suppression
  lints in it need `rust-version` 1.81 or later.

## 3. Ownership and borrowing

**Prefer unique ownership.** Reach for `Rc`/`Arc` only when shared ownership is part of
the design, and for `RefCell`/`Mutex` only when interior mutability is. They are not
failures, but they move checking from compile time to run time, so use them on purpose.

**Don't clone to make the borrow checker stop complaining.** A clone that exists only to
end a borrow produces a silent copy whose later changes are lost. Try these first, in
roughly this order:

1. Extend a temporary with a named `let`, or shorten a borrow with a block.
2. Split a long expression into typed intermediates so the failing step is visible.
3. Move a field out of `&mut self` with `std::mem::take` (needs `Default`),
   `std::mem::replace`, or `Option::take` instead of cloning it.
4. Split a large struct into smaller ones so disjoint fields can be borrowed separately.
   The compiler tracks disjoint field borrows inside one function, but not across
   method calls.
5. Clone small, immutable data deliberately, and say so in a comment if it's not obvious.
6. Use indices into an owning `Vec`, or `Rc<RefCell<_>>` with `Weak` back-pointers, as
   a last resort. Avoid self-referential structs.

```rust
// Move out of a &mut enum without cloning.
fn a_to_b(e: &mut MyEnum) {
    if let MyEnum::A { name, x: 0 } = e {
        *e = MyEnum::B { name: std::mem::take(name) };
    }
}
```

**Accept the most general borrowed type.** `&str` not `&String`, `&[T]` not `&Vec<T>`,
`&T` not `&Box<T>`, `Option<&T>` not `&Option<T>`. Deref coercion then lets callers pass
owned values, borrows, or literals. Where you only read a path, string, or byte buffer,
`impl AsRef<Path>` / `impl AsRef<str>` / `impl AsRef<[u8]>` is fine on parameters (never
on struct fields; store `PathBuf` and `String`). Library code that only iterates should
take `impl IntoIterator<Item = T>`; application code may simply take `&[T]`.

**Take ownership only when you need it, and then take it by value.** If a function stores
or consumes its argument, take `T`, not `&T` plus an internal `.clone()`. If it only
reads, take `&T`; if it mutates in place, `&mut T`. Return multiple values as a tuple or
struct, not through `&mut` out-parameters (reusing a caller-owned buffer, as
`Read::read` does, is the exception).

**Prefer owned data in structs.** A struct holding `&'a T` forces a lifetime onto every
container. Owning a `String` or `Vec<u8>` is usually simpler and rarely the bottleneck.
When a type does carry a lifetime, give it a descriptive name (`'src`, `'conn`); `'_` and
`'a` are fine on simple functions.

**Freeze after setup.** Build with `let mut`, then rebind `let data = data;` so later
code cannot mutate it by accident.

**Keep `Rc`, `Arc`, `Box`, and `RefCell` out of public signatures.** Take `&T`,
`&mut T`, or `T` and let callers decide how to own things. A service that must be shared
implements a cheap `Clone` by wrapping its state in `Arc<Inner>` internally.

## 4. Types and API design

### Naming

| Item | Case | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Types, traits, enum variants | `UpperCamelCase` | Acronyms are one word: `Uuid`, `HttpClient` |
| Functions, methods, modules, locals | `snake_case` | |
| Constants, statics | `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` | |
| Type parameters | short, from the main bound | `T`, `R: Read`, `W: Write` |
| Lifetimes | short lowercase | descriptive when on a type |

- No `get_` prefix on getters: `fn len(&self)`, `fn name(&self) -> &str`,
  `fn name_mut(&mut self)`. Use bare `get` only when there is one obvious thing to get
  (`Cell::get`). Related: `set_foo(T)`, `take_foo()`, `with_foo(|f| ..)` for closure
  access, and unsafe `_unchecked` siblings for checked accessors.
- Conversion prefixes signal cost and ownership: `as_` (free, borrow to borrow), `to_`
  (expensive, borrow to owned or borrow to borrow), `into_` (consumes `self`). Put `mut`
  in type order: `as_mut_slice`, not `as_slice_mut`.
- Constructors: `new` (primary), `with_capacity` / `new_with_foo` (variants), `try_new`
  (fallible), `from_foo` (conversion; pair important ones with a `From` impl). I/O
  resources use domain verbs: `File::open`, `TcpStream::connect`.
- `iter` / `iter_mut` / `into_iter` return types named `Iter` / `IterMut` / `IntoIter`;
  `keys()` returns `Keys`.
- Error types read verb-object-error: `ParseBoolError`, not `BoolParseError`.
- Avoid weasel suffixes `Service`, `Manager`, `Factory`, `Helper`, `Util`. Name the thing
  it is (`Bookings`, `Dispatcher`, `FooBuilder`). Don't repeat the module name in the
  type (`foo::Id`, not `foo::FooId`). Avoid abbreviations an outsider wouldn't know.
- If you implement `len()`, implement `is_empty()`.
- Feature names are bare: `std`, `serde`, `alloc`, never `use-std` or `no-std`.

### Model the domain with types

- **Newtypes** for semantic distinctions: `struct Miles(f64)` and `struct Kilometers(f64)`
  cannot be mixed, where a type alias can. Add `#[repr(transparent)]` when layout matters,
  and derive or forward the traits you need (`derive_more` cuts the boilerplate). A
  newtype that encodes an invariant (`Month`) validates in a fallible constructor
  (`TryFrom`, `FromStr`, `try_new`) and never offers an infallible `From` from the raw type.
- **No `bool` parameters in public or shared signatures.** `report(true)` is unreadable at
  the call site and cannot grow a third mode. Use a two-variant enum
  (`Verbosity::Summary`, `Verbosity::Full`) or two methods (`report()`,
  `report_verbose()`): `Widget::new(Size::Small, Shape::Round)`, not
  `Widget::new(true, false)`. The only exception is a private helper whose call sites sit
  a few lines away. When refactoring, an existing `bool` parameter is one of the smells to
  remove, not a detail to preserve.
- **Named fields over tuples**, except single-field newtypes and very local code.
- **`Option` for absence, never sentinels** such as `-1` or `""`. **Data-carrying enums**
  instead of "field X is only meaningful when Y is set".
- **Use the strongest std type:** `PathBuf` / `&Path` for paths, `Duration` for spans,
  `NonZeroU32` internally only (keep plain integers at API boundaries).
- **Independent flags** use the `bitflags` crate; an enum models exactly one choice.

### Derive and implement the standard traits eagerly

Downstream crates cannot add std traits to your types (orphan rule), so you must. Derive
whenever every field supports it: `Debug` (on every public type; hand-write it to redact
secrets), `Clone` (except unique resources and key material), `Copy` (only small
bitwise-copyable types, because the compiler copies silently), `PartialEq` / `Eq`,
`PartialOrd` / `Ord` (never ship `PartialOrd` without `Ord` when a total order exists),
`Hash` (consistent with `Eq`), `Default`. Implement `Display` for anything meant to be
read: error types, string-like wrappers. Add `#[must_use]` to pure functions and to
types, such as errors and lazy values, whose discarding is a bug.

Implement `From` / `TryFrom`, never `Into` / `TryInto` directly (blanket impls give you
those). Prefer `from` / `into` over `as`, which silently allows lossy casts. Implement
`FromStr` rather than an ad-hoc `from_str` method, `FromIterator` and `Extend` on
collections, and `IntoIterator` for both owned and borrowed forms. Implement `Deref` only
on smart pointers and owning collections (`Vec<T>` to `[T]`), never to fake inheritance.
Overload operators only for their mathematical meaning.

Don't put derivable trait bounds on struct definitions: `#[derive(Clone)] struct Good<T>`,
not `struct Bad<T: Clone + Debug>`. Bounds belong on the `impl` blocks that need them.

If you hand-write `Ord`, hand-write `PartialEq`, `PartialOrd`, and `Hash` to agree with it
(compare the same fields, ignore the same fields). A derived `PartialEq` next to a custom
`Ord` breaks the std contract and misbehaves in `BTreeMap` and `sort`/`dedup`. Say in the
docs which fields equality ignores.

### Constructors, builders, defaults

- Provide `new()` even when `Default` exists, and make them agree (one delegates to the
  other). Derive or implement `Default` so callers can write `..Default::default()`;
  bag-of-options structs with public fields should always have it.
- Up to two optional parameters: inherent constructors (`new`, `with_a`, `with_b`).
  Beyond that, or when construction validates or has side effects, add a builder:
  `Foo::builder()` returns `FooBuilder`, setters are named after fields (`timeout(d)`,
  not `set_timeout`) and infallible, and `build() -> Result<Foo, Error>` does all
  validation including cross-field checks. Prefer non-consuming setters
  (`&mut self -> &mut Self`) unless `build` must move a value out.
- A constructor with four or more loose arguments should group them into semantic types:
  `Deposit::new(account, amount)` rather than four `&str` / `u64` parameters.

### Visibility and evolution

- Private by default. Fields stay private unless the struct is passive C-style data.
  Widen to `pub(crate)` or `pub(super)` before `pub`. Making an item more public later is
  non-breaking; the reverse is breaking, and every `pub` item is a promise.
- Mark public enums and public-field structs that cross crate boundaries
  `#[non_exhaustive]` unless the set is a stable ontology. When matching one, list the
  variants you handle and add a wildcard arm.
- Seal traits you don't want implemented downstream, and say so in the docs:

  ```rust
  pub trait TheTrait: private::Sealed { /* ... */ }
  mod private {
      pub trait Sealed {}
      impl Sealed for usize {}
  }
  ```

- Hide implementation iterator types behind `impl Iterator<Item = T>` (internal APIs) or
  a newtype (public APIs you must keep stable).
- Expose each public item at exactly one path. Don't `pub use` a foreign crate's items
  unless you are an umbrella crate. Avoid leaking third-party types into your public API;
  feature-gate `serde` impls behind a feature named `serde`. If a dependency's type must
  appear, re-export it so callers can name the matching version.
- Mark a function `const` only if it will stay `const`. Don't expose `ErrorKind` enums
  or other internals that lock in failure modes you consider private.

### Traits and generics

- Define a trait only for generic programming (`T: Trait`, `impl Trait`, `dyn Trait`) or
  as an extension trait (`FooExt`). Don't use traits merely to organize code. Put
  essential functionality in inherent methods and have trait impls forward to them, so
  callers need no import.
- Prefer, in order: concrete types; generics (`T: Trait`, `impl Trait`); `dyn Trait`,
  ideally wrapped in your own struct (`struct DynStore(Arc<dyn Store>)`). Generics give
  static dispatch and inlining; trait objects give heterogeneous collections and smaller
  binaries. Don't nest generics on service-level types (`Service<Backend>` is fine;
  `Service<Backend<Store>>` is not).
- Decide early whether a trait must be object-safe. Generic methods or `Self` outside the
  receiver break it; exclude such methods with `where Self: Sized`.
- Keep required trait methods minimal and provide defaults for everything derivable from
  them, as `Iterator` does from `next`.
- If a function has a clear receiver, make it a method. A computation with no receiver is
  a free function, not `Database::check(params)`. Associated functions are for
  construction.
- Closures: use the most general bound that works (`FnOnce` if called once, `FnMut` if it
  mutates, else `Fn`) and prefer `Fn*` bounds to bare `fn` pointers. Closure parameters go
  last; don't take more than one.
- Keep parameter order consistent across a crate: call-specific first, ubiquitous
  context (loggers, allocators) last.
- Reach for a macro only when functions, generics, and traits cannot do the job. Prefer
  `macro_rules!` to proc macros, make macro input look like the output it generates, and
  never let a macro change a type's kind or a function's signature.

### Refactoring someone else's code

- Fix every smell the request is about, not just the cheap ones: clones that only
  satisfy the borrow checker, `&String` / `&Vec<T>` parameters, `unwrap` on fallible
  paths, `Rc<RefCell<_>>` in signatures, `get_` getters, `bool` parameters, `+` string
  concatenation, `#![deny(warnings)]`, error types without `Error`, nondeterministic
  `HashMap` iteration in output.
- Keep public behavior identical unless changing it is the point: the same operations,
  the same success and failure semantics, the same output bytes. Turning a panic into an
  `Err` is the change callers want. Dropping an error variant, removing a derive, or
  changing what a constructor takes is not; if a signature must change, show the before
  and after in the change list and say why.
- Preserve quirks you don't understand and flag them, rather than silently "fixing" them.
- When the module has no tests, pin the current behavior with a few before you touch it.

## 5. Errors and panics

Pick the mechanism by contract:

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Absence is normal (`first()`, `checked_add`) | `Option<T>` |
| The caller may need to know what went wrong | `Result<T, E>` |
| A bug or violated invariant inside your code | `panic!` / `assert!` / `expect("why")` |

**Panics are not exceptions.** A panic means "stop now". Never use one to report bad
input, never rely on `catch_unwind` for control flow (it does nothing under
`panic = "abort"` and can leave state inconsistent), and never catch a panic and continue
inside a library. Where a panicking convenience is justified, pair it with a fallible API
(`get` / `get_unchecked`, `new` / `try_new`) and document it under `# Panics`.

**Every intentional panic carries a message with the relevant values:**
`assert!(buf.len() >= HEADER, "buffer too small: {} bytes", buf.len())`,
`expect("config is loaded before workers start")`. Prefer `expect("reason")` to
`unwrap()`. Don't restate the condition as the message.

**Pattern-match instead of check-then-unwrap:** `if let Some(v) = opt { .. }` or
`let Some(v) = opt else { return .. };`, never `if opt.is_some() { opt.unwrap() }`.

**Lock poisoning is fatal:** `.lock().expect("lock poisoned")`. Don't recover with
`into_inner`.

**Library error types** (any `E` in a public `Result`):

- Implement `std::error::Error` (which requires `Debug` + `Display`), be
  `Send + Sync + 'static`, and implement `source()` for wrapped causes. Never use `()`,
  `String`, or `Box<dyn Error>` as a library's public error type.
- `Display` messages are lowercase, concise, and have no trailing punctuation:
  `"invalid header length"`.
- Implement `From<Upstream>` so `?` converts. Use `map_err` only for foreign errors or
  to add context.
- Two sound shapes: an enum with one variant per cause (`thiserror` generates this
  well), or a struct per situation with a private `kind` plus `is_xxx()` and accessor
  methods. Either way, don't make one crate-wide enum that lists every failure mode in
  the crate, and don't expose details callers cannot act on.
- If a fallible function consumes an argument, return it inside the error so the caller
  can retry without cloning (`FromUtf8Error::into_bytes`).
- Never expose `anyhow::Error` in a library's public API.

**Application error handling:** `anyhow` or `eyre` with `.context("opening config")` is
the right tool. Use one app-level error type, not several. `main` may return
`Result<(), anyhow::Error>`.

**Destructors never fail, panic, or block.** Provide `close(self) -> Result<()>` for
fallible teardown and let `Drop` do best-effort cleanup.

**Document failure modes:** `# Errors` for any `Result`, `# Panics` for any reachable
panic, `# Safety` for every `unsafe fn`.

## 6. Everyday idioms

- **Iterators over hand loops** when the pipeline is short and reads top-down:
  `values.iter().filter(..).map(..).collect()`, `.any()`, `.sum()`, `.fold()`. Collect
  fallible steps into `Result<Vec<_>, E>` and apply `?`. Keep an explicit `for` loop when
  the body is large, does several jobs, or needs awkward early returns. Bind a long chain
  to a named variable rather than putting it in a `for` header, and prefer `for x in it`
  to `.for_each(|x| ..)`.
- **`Option` / `Result` combinators** (`map`, `and_then`, `ok_or_else`, `unwrap_or_else`,
  `as_ref`, `as_deref`) when they're clearer than `match`, and `match` when they're not.
- **`format!` / `write!`** with inline args (`format!("{name}: {count}")`) for
  concatenation and substitution, not chained `+` or `str::replace`. `write!` into an
  existing buffer in hot paths.
- **Explicit types where inference obscures intent:** on `.into()`, `.parse()`,
  `.collect()`, and complex iterator results. Prefer `let x: Vec<u32> = ..` to a turbofish.
- **Drop guards for cleanup** that must run on early return or unwind. Bind them to a
  name (`let _guard = ..`), because `let _ = ..` drops immediately.
- **Closures that capture mixed ownership:** rebind in a block, then `move`:

  ```rust
  let job = {
      let cfg = cfg.clone();
      move || run(cfg, data)
  };
  ```

- **Import style:** one `use` per module path (`use foo::bar::{Bar, Baz};`); types and
  traits imported and used unqualified (`Regex`); free functions qualified by their module
  (`mem::take`, `fs::read`). Import a trait inside the function that needs it unless the
  whole file uses it. No glob imports except `use super::*` in test modules and
  `use Enum::*` inside a function that matches on it.
- **Magic numbers** become named `const`s with a doc comment saying where the value
  comes from and what changing it affects.
- **Logging:** structured events through `tracing` or `log`, not `println!` / `dbg!`,
  except for a CLI's own stdout output.

## 7. Concurrency and async

- Public types, and the futures they return, should be `Send` (and usually `Sync`). Pin
  it with a compile-time check so a refactor can't silently regress it:

  ```rust
  const _: () = {
      const fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
      assert_send::<MyClient>();
  };
  ```

  Holding an `Rc` or a `RefCell` borrow across an `.await` makes a future `!Send`.
- Prefer message passing (channels) to shared state. When sharing is necessary: keep data
  with linked invariants under one lock, keep lock scopes to a few lines, never call user
  closures while holding a lock, and never return a `MutexGuard` from a public method.
- Write `async fn` rather than `fn -> impl Future`, except in traits or when setup must
  run outside the async block for a hot path.
- Long CPU-bound work inside async must yield (`tokio::task::yield_now().await` every
  tens of microseconds) or move to `spawn_blocking`.
- Library code doesn't spawn raw threads or assume a runtime; take an executor, a spawn
  function, or `impl AsyncRead` / `impl Read` from the caller.

## 8. Unsafe and FFI

- Write `unsafe` only for one of three reasons: a novel abstraction safe code can't
  express, a benchmarked performance need, or FFI and platform calls. Reach for std and
  well-reviewed crates first; they already contain the audited `unsafe`.
- Every `unsafe` block or impl gets a `// SAFETY:` comment stating why the invariants
  hold. Every `unsafe fn` gets a `# Safety` doc section listing what the caller must
  uphold. Enable `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn`.
- Keep `unsafe` in the smallest module that can uphold its invariant and wrap it in a
  safe API; the module boundary is the soundness boundary. A safe function that can cause
  undefined behavior through any sequence of safe calls is unsound, and unsound code is
  never acceptable.
- Mark a function `unsafe` only when misuse can cause undefined behavior, not because it
  is dangerous (`delete_database()` is a safe function).
- No `transmute` to cast enums or dodge lifetimes, and no `unsafe impl Send` to silence
  the compiler.
- Test unsafe code under Miri and with adversarial inputs.
- FFI: `#[repr(C)]` on shared structs, sized integer types, `CString` / `CStr` for
  strings, allocate and free on the same side, wrap C-owned pointers in an RAII type whose
  `Drop` frees them, check for null and return `Result`, and stop panics at the boundary
  with `catch_unwind`. Generate bindings with `bindgen` in a `foo-sys` crate and keep
  business logic in a safe core crate.

## 9. Crates, modules, dependencies

- **Prefer small, single-purpose crates** in a flat `crates/` workspace; never nest a
  crate inside another crate's `src/`. Split when a crate grows a second purpose or a
  subdirectory. Share versions and lints through `[workspace.dependencies]` and
  `[workspace.lints]`.
- **Modules:** name a leaf module after its primary item (`Foo` lives in `foo.rs`).
  Non-leaf modules contain only `mod` declarations and re-exports. Put the essential items
  at the crate root and group the rest by use case (`account`, `network`), not by kind
  (`traits`, `errors`). Don't define a prelude.
- **Re-export individually** (`pub use foo::{A, B};`), never with a glob.
- **Dependencies:** every one costs compile time, binary size, and supply-chain exposure,
  including `build.rs` and proc macros. Use ranges (`"1"`, `"1.4"`), never `"*"` or a
  needless `"="`. Commit `Cargo.lock` for binaries. Audit with `cargo tree --duplicates`,
  `cargo deny`, `cargo udeps`, and `cargo audit`.
- **Features are additive and bare-named:** `std`, `serde`, `alloc`, `test-util`. Never
  `no-std`, `use-serde`, or a feature that removes or changes a public item. Don't
  feature-gate struct fields or trait methods. Put mocks and fakes behind `test-util`.
- **Semver:** breaking changes include removing or renaming public items, adding a
  variant to an enum that isn't `#[non_exhaustive]`, adding a field to a publicly
  constructible struct, adding a trait bound, or making a trait non-object-safe.
  Deprecate in a minor release before removing in a major one. Use the latest stable
  edition for new crates and set an MSRV deliberately.
- Don't run code before `main()` (no `ctor`-style crates). Don't use unstable features
  on a stable toolchain.

## 10. Documentation and comments

- `///` on every public item; `//!` at the top of every public module and the crate root.
  The first sentence is a single line of about fifteen words, because it becomes the
  summary in listings.
- Sections, in this order, as applicable: `# Examples`, `# Errors`, `# Panics`,
  `# Safety`. Examples use `?` with the `fn main` hidden behind `# ` lines, never
  `unwrap()`, because users copy them verbatim. Describe parameters in prose, not a table.
- Document what the signature can't say: preconditions, side effects, ownership
  transfer, complexity, and why. Don't restate the type or the name;
  `/// Removes an element.` on `remove_element` is noise.
- Link items with `` [`Type`] ``. Hide impls users never trigger
  (`From<PrivateError> for PublicError`) with `#[doc(hidden)]`.
- `//` comments explain why, not what: `// SAFETY:`, `// TODO(issue-123):`, non-obvious
  magic values, workarounds with a link. No design journals, "why we chose X" essays, or
  rule-compliance tables in code docs. Document the end state.

## 11. Tests

- Unit tests in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; .. }` for private internals.
  Integration tests in `tests/` for anything reachable through the public API, and prefer
  that location when either would do. Doc examples are tests too.
- Test observable behavior and properties (monotonic, round-trips, idempotent), not
  restated constants or mirrored branches.
- Write a failing test before fixing a bug. Cover each feature combination and each
  platform-specific path.
- Anything doing I/O, time, randomness, or network must be mockable:
  `new_mocked() -> (Self, MockCtrl)` behind `test-util`, not a `Default` that performs I/O.
- Fuzz parsers of untrusted input with `cargo fuzz`. Benchmark with `criterion` or `divan`
  and `std::hint::black_box`. Run Miri over `unsafe`.
- Assertions get context so failures read well: `assert_eq!(got, want, "input {input:?}")`.

## 12. Performance, in order

Design for usability first and optimize after measuring. When you do: `Vec::with_capacity`
or `collect()` over push loops; reuse caller-owned buffers in hot APIs
(`fn read_into(&mut self, buf: &mut Vec<u8>)`); `Box<[T]>`, `Box<str>`, `Arc<str>` for
long-lived immutable sequences; `shrink_to_fit` on long-lived collections built without a
reservation; a faster hasher (`foldhash`, `FxHash`) only for trusted keys; batch work
instead of per-item locking; applications may set a `#[global_allocator]` such as
`mimalloc`. Derive `Copy` for small plain types and never for large ones.

## 13. Final checklist

Before returning Rust code, confirm:

- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test` are clean.
- No `unwrap()` outside tests and `main`; every `expect`, `assert`, and `panic` has a
  message with the relevant values.
- Public functions take `&str`, `&[T]`, `impl AsRef<_>`, or `impl IntoIterator`, not
  `&String` or `&Vec<T>`.
- Every public type derives `Debug` and the applicable common traits; error types
  implement `Error + Display + Send + Sync + 'static`.
- No `bool` parameters in public signatures; no hand-written `Ord` without matching
  `PartialEq` and `Hash`.
- No `.clone()` whose only job is to satisfy the borrow checker.
- No glob imports, no preludes, no glob re-exports, no leaked third-party types.
- Every `unsafe` block has a `// SAFETY:` comment; every `unsafe fn` has `# Safety` docs.
- Public items have docs with a one-line summary and `# Errors` / `# Panics` where relevant.
- Application code stayed simple; library code followed the API rules.

## References

Read these when you need the reasoning behind a rule or a complete checklist for a task.
Each is a condensed digest of one source.

- `references/rust-api-guidelines.md` (https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/):
  designing a public API or crate; all 54 checklist items with conventions.
- `references/effective-rust.md` (https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/): choosing
  between alternatives: generics vs `dyn`, `Result` vs panic, iterators vs loops,
  borrow-checker tactics, dependencies, CI.
- `references/rust-design-patterns.md` (https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/):
  idioms, patterns, and anti-patterns with code.
- `references/microsoft-rust-guidelines.md` (https://microsoft.github.io/rust-guidelines/):
  error struct design, panic policy, unsafe policy, async, workspace layout, performance.
- `references/google-rust-style-guide.md` (https://google.github.io/styleguide/rustguide.html):
  formatting, imports, module layout, accessor naming, application vs library.

# Build with TypeSafe (Jev)

Use when a feature needs programmable structured decisions (routing, ranking, extraction, verification) instead of LLM prompt-and-parse.

## Source of truth
Read live docs from https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and relevant `.md` pages before integrating.

## Core idea
System One / **Jev**: send `state` + typed questions → Choice / Score / Noul with probabilities. Code owns workflow; model supplies judgments. Endpoint `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`. Pin model versions (e.g. `jev-1.13.0`). Auth: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` Bearer. Input priced; output free.

## Design
- Keep rules, math, dates, lookups in code.
- One narrow judgment per question; many questions in one request (parallel).
- Choice = one of set; Noul = yes/no probability; Score = degree on rubric.
- Use confidence for thresholds; validate on user data.
- Never put API keys in client/browser.

## WM spike context
For Walrus Memory WALM-654: post-recall top-K rerank/routing only; synthetic data by default; fail closed if Jev unavailable.

# WALM ticket template

Use linear-mysten only (Mysten Labs, WALM team). Template: linear.app/mysten-labs/team/WALM/new?template=... (Thanos's). Draft first and show the user before creating unless they said to create directly.

## Fields (fill every one)
1. **Title**: start with the surface in brackets: [Relayer], [SDK], [MCP], [Dashboard], [Ops], [Docs]. Then the outcome (what is true when done), not the task.
2. **Problem**: what is wrong or missing today, who hits it, evidence (user report, GitHub issue, log line, review finding, Slack thread). Facts, not the fix.
3. **Desired behavior**: what the user or calling app sees when done, from their side, with exact copy, error text or API response where it matters.
4. **Scope**: list by surface (relayer, SDK, MCP, dashboard, config, tests). Call out any migration, flag, contract change or rollout step.
5. **Out of scope**: what it deliberately does not do and where that lives (ticket id or "not planned").
6. **Acceptance criteria**: one checkable statement per line, verifiable without asking. End with a Demo line: where it is shown (`dev`, test account, script — note: `staging` is retired; `dev` and `production` are the only active environments) and what the reviewer sees.
7. **Proposed estimate**: story points on the CommandOSS SP scale, including code review effort. Above 5 means split the ticket. Always set before starting work.
8. **Blocked by**: ticket ids or a named decision, or "none, can start immediately".
9. **Source**: link to where it came from (Slack thread, GitHub issue, meeting and date, review finding, user report, parent ticket).

## GitHub issue & PR linking
When the ticket comes from or relates to a GitHub issue or PR:
- Put the full GitHub issue URL in Source and attach it to the Linear issue (`create_attachment`, or links on `save_issue`).
- Ask the user before commenting the Linear ticket link back on the GitHub issue (it posts as them).
- **NEVER expose internal `WALM-*` IDs on public GitHub**:
  - Do **not** use `walm-*` or `WALM-*` in GitHub branch names (use `fix/issue-<N>-<slug>` or `fix/<slug>` instead).
  - Do **not** include `WALM-*` in GitHub PR titles, PR bodies, commit messages, code comments, or changelogs (`CHANGELOG.md` / `changelog.mdx`).
  - On GitHub PRs, reference only the public GitHub issue (e.g. `Fixes #<N>` in the PR body and `(#<N>)` in changelogs).
  - Instead, post/attach the GitHub PR URL **on the Linear `WALM-*` ticket** (via `save_comment` / `create_attachment` / `save_issue` on `linear-mysten`) and update the Linear ticket status there.

## Parallel Post-Merge Reconciliation (`walm-ticket` + `gh-issue-fixed` + `memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet`)
Whenever a PR that solves a GitHub issue has **100% CI checks GREEN (`SUCCESS`)** and **`APPROVED`** review and is merged into `dev`, execute these three steps in parallel:
1. **`walm-ticket` (Linear `linear-mysten`)**: Move the `WALM-*` ticket(s) to **`Done`** (`save_issue`) and post a comment (`save_comment`) with the merged PR URL, merge commit SHA, release version, and closed GitHub issue(s).
2. **`gh-issue-fixed` (GitHub Issue)**: Post the merged-fix reply on every GitHub issue solved by the PR (never mentioning `WALM-*`) and close the GitHub issue (`gh issue close <N> --repo MystenLabs/MemWal` if still `OPEN`).
3. **`memwal-review` + `memwal-dev-wallet` (`dev` Verification)**: Verify the `dev` deployment (`https://relayer.dev.memwal.ai/version`, `/health`, Railway `dev` logs, and `memwal-dev-wallet` E2E check) to confirm the merged changes run cleanly on `dev`.

## Retired Standalone Demo Apps (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`)
- The standalone demo applications (`apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, `apps/researcher`) are **disabled and no longer maintained** (note: `apps/app`, the core Dashboard / Playground web console, remains actively maintained).
- Do **not** create or implement new `WALM-*` tickets for `apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, or `apps/researcher`.
- If an existing open `WALM-*` ticket targets `apps/chatbot`, `apps/noter`, or `apps/researcher`, move it to **`Canceled`** on Linear with a comment explaining that the standalone demo app is retired and no longer maintained, close any associated open PR, and close the corresponding GitHub issue (`--reason "not planned"`) using the retired demo app reply in `gh-issue-fixed`.

## Before creating
- Search existing WALM issues for duplicates.
- Verify linear-mysten is the WALM workspace, not CommandOSS.

# Boost (`/boost`) — Multi-Agent Orchestrator for Gemini 4 Argon

This skill brings Antigravity's `/boost` (`teamwork_preview` / `teamwork_orchestrator`) multi-agent swarm workflow to **Gemini 4 Argon** across both:
1. **T3 Code (`zroute` provider / `zroute/gemini-4-argon` on Pi runtime)** via T3's `orchestrator_capabilities` + `delegate_task`
2. **Antigravity CLI (`agy`)** via native `/boost` (`teamwork_interviewer` -> `teamwork_orchestrator` -> worker/auditor subagents)

## How to invoke

- **Slash command (T3 Code `zroute` or `agy` CLI):**
  ```text
  /boost <your task or feature request>
  /boost [skip-interview] <your task or feature request>
  ```
- **Inline skill chip (T3 Code):**
  ```text
  $boost <your task or feature request>
  /skill:boost <your task or feature request>
  ```

## Execution Protocol (when running on `zroute/gemini-4-argon` in T3 Code / Pi)

### Phase 1 — Scope & Interview Gate (`[skip-interview]` supported)
1. If the user's request has critical ambiguities **and** does not include `[skip-interview]` (or "do all", "handle all", "autonomous"):
   - Write `.agents/teamwork/interviewer/prompt_draft.md` capturing the request verbatim and listing concise `[OPEN: ...]` questions.
   - Ask the user the minimal clarifying questions needed before spawning workers.
2. If the request is clear or includes `[skip-interview]` / autonomous execution intent:
   - Proceed directly to Phase 2 without blocking on questions.

### Phase 2 — Teamwork Workspace Initialization (`.agents/teamwork/`)
Record authoritative state files in `.agents/teamwork/`:
1. **`.agents/teamwork/ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md`** — Verbatim user request, active constraints, and integrity mode (`Development` or `Demo`).
2. **`.agents/teamwork/BRIEFING.md`** — Codebase architecture summary, affected modules, acceptance criteria, and verification commands.
3. **`.agents/teamwork/DISPATCH.md`** — Workstream decomposition table assigning disjoint file scopes and verification targets to each subagent.

### Phase 3 — Parallel Multi-Agent Dispatch on `zroute/gemini-4-argon`
1. Call `orchestrator_capabilities` once to confirm the active `zroute` provider instance (`zroute-native`) and model (`zroute/gemini-4-argon`).
2. For independent workstreams (survey, implementation, tests/QA), spawn child agents via `delegate_task`:
   - `role`: `"research"`, `"implementation"`, `"test"`, or `"review"`
   - `target`: `{ providerInstanceId: "zroute-native", model: "zroute/gemini-4-argon", options: { thinking: "high" } }`
   - Give each worker its exact assignment from `.agents/teamwork/DISPATCH.md` and point it to `.agents/teamwork/ORIGINAL_REQUEST.md`.
   - Use `isolation: "worktree"` only when parallel workers would otherwise edit overlapping files; use `isolation: "shared"` when file scopes are strictly disjoint.

### Phase 4 — Integrity Audit & Empirical Verification Gate
Before reporting completion:
1. **No Facades / No Hardcoded Outputs:** Verify every changed file maintains real state and genuine runtime behavior.
2. **Empirical Suite Execution:** Run the project's real build, typecheck, and verification commands end-to-end (for `near-ai-chat`: `pnpm check:near`, `pnpm sandbox:probe`, `pnpm check:cases`, `pnpm check:tools`, `pnpm eval`).
3. **Synthesize Deliverable:** Summarize completed workstreams, verification evidence, and updated files.
