interface-bts.markdown:
---
name: interface-bts
description: Draws a spec poster of an interaction you point it at, with the real component paused at its key moments and every duration, curve and size read from it and drawn in place.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# interface-bts

This skill turns one interaction in a project into an A4 spec poster: the behind-the-scenes drawing of how it moves. The poster has:
- **Figure 1:** the real component, frozen mid-motion, with its sizes dimensioned on it.
- **Callouts:** numbered parts, with a note for each saying what changes and why.
- **Figure 2:** the curve or mapping that drives it.
- **Moments:** a row you can pick to re-drive the component.
- **Specification:** trigger, properties, duration, easing and reduced motion.

A reader should leave with one sentence about how it works.

The poster documents what the interface does now. It isn't a redesign, a live debug overlay or a video. If someone wants a component changed, say so and leave the poster out of it. Every number on the poster comes from the running component; anything that can't be read is marked as an estimate, never filled in.

Example: `/interface-bts the dropdown in components/menu.tsx`

## 1. Study the interaction

- Find the component, its callers, its styles, its handlers and its animation code. Run it and use the interaction yourself.
- Trace input → decision → output:
  - What triggers it?
  - What changes?
  - Which values drive the change (durations, easings, thresholds, sizes)?
  - Where does each value live?
- Probe the cases that show the rules: a slow input, a reversal, an interruption, the resting state, and reduced motion.

**Done when** you can name the mechanism in one sentence and point to the source of each value it uses.

## 2. Agree the poster in chat

List these and wait for a yes before building:

- **Headline:** the mechanism in plain words ("The pill catches up: its left edge and width ease on one curve").
- **Hero moment:** the frame where the mechanism shows most. Usually mid-motion or just past a threshold, rarely at rest.
- **Moments:** 3–5 in story order (rest, start, the hero, past it, settled).
- **Callouts:** 2–4 numbered parts on figure 1, with what each note will say.
- **Figure 2:** pick from the table below.
- **Measurements:** the one or two sizes the headline depends on.

| To explain | Figure 2 draws |
| --- | --- |
| How a value travels over time (most transitions) | The easing curve, with the held moment marked on it |
| Two things on one clock (a cross-fade, an icon swap) | Both curves on one time axis |
| A value that follows input (a drag, a scroll) | Input mapped to output, with the clamp and snap points |
| Keyframes or a loop | The keyframe stops over one cycle |
| A threshold or snap | The decision regions, with the current input inside them |

**Done when** the user has agreed the headline and the moments.

## 3. Freeze the real component

- **Figure 1 is the real component.** Drive it with its own handlers, and freeze it by pausing its real animations: `getAnimations()`, then `pause()` and set `currentTime`, or seek the animation library's own timeline. Never rebuild it, and never run a second animation to imitate it.
- **Read every number from the running component:** computed style, `getAnimations()`, its timeline, or data attributes it publishes. Never type a duration, an easing or a threshold into the poster. Take the first timing function with `firstEasing()`: splitting a computed list on commas cuts `cubic-bezier()` in half.
- **A component that isn't a CSS transition needs its own driver,** and some fight the poster: anything placed by floating-ui (Radix menus, popovers, tooltips), fixed to the window (toasters, sheets), measuring itself on screen (drag and swipe thresholds), or moving focus. Read [references/drivers.md](references/drivers.md) before building one of these.
- **Check that channels agree before you show them as one mechanism,** for example that opacity follows the same curve as scale. If they don't, the poster shows its error state rather than a wrong drawing.
- **Moments are copies:** static DOM snapshots with computed styles inlined, and inert. Use one camera for all of them, so growth never reads as shrinkage.
- **Report what you measured,** even when it contradicts what the code intends.

**Done when** each moment re-drives the component to the same frame every time, the held values match the source, and (for a driven gesture or pointer path) one run has been checked against a real browser mouse or touch.

## 4. Compose the poster

- **Always A4 portrait.** Lay it out once on a 794 × 1123 artboard (A4 at 96 dpi), then scale the whole poster to fit the space, centred. Never reflow at a breakpoint: a resize changes the scale, not the arrangement.
- **Order:** the component's name, figure 1 with its moments under it, then the foot. In the foot, the notes and figure 2 sit side by side, and the specification spans the width below them. A title block at the very bottom states the units, the drawing scale and the line types, once.
- **Type:**
  - the name at 16px, weight 500, as the only heading;
  - notes and specification at 13/18;
  - 12px inside drawings;
  - one font, sentence case, nothing heavier than 600;
  - tabular digits, with units lighter than their numbers.
- **Padding:** 20px top and bottom, 32px at the sides.
- **Size each drawing to its slot.** Measure the free height, then pick the drawing scale so the component and its dimensions fit. State it ("drawn at 3×").
- **No housing.** No cards or boxes round notes or figures; use hairlines and flat fills. No glows, no large blurred shadows, no gradients for depth.
- **Accent:**
  - Each poster takes one iOS 26 system colour (`IOS26` in the kit), unique across the project's posters. Record it in `SPEC_ACCENTS`.
  - Once all twelve are taken, reuse the least-used one.
  - The accent marks lines and fills, with a 12% tint under the run. Words use a darker ink of the same hue (lightness capped at 0.52), so yellow and mint stay readable.
- **Theme:** use the app's real theme. Pass `theme="dark"` only when the app itself is dark, read through its own mechanism. Never invent a dark theme, and never put a theme toggle on the poster. Draw nothing until the theme is known, and key the poster on it so a change redraws it and copies the moments again.

Drafting conventions (dimensions from a datum, line types, detail views, aligned views) are in [references/drafting.md](references/drafting.md). Read it before drawing.

**Done when** everything on the poster has a slot and no word sits on the component.

## 5. Polish, then verify by measurement

Polish:
- **Optical alignment:** note numbers sit on their first line's baseline, the foot's columns share a first baseline, and notes and figures share left edges.
- **Concentric radii:** an outline drawn round a part uses the part's own radius at the drawing scale. Anything nested uses the outer radius minus the gap.
- **Soft ends:** drafting grids fade out radially, and the moments row fades at both ends. Dimmed moments blur slightly as they fade.
- **Leaders** leave their parts at 45°, or run straight across where a gap is the only clear path.
- **Hovering a note** dims every part tagged with another note.

Verify:
- **Overlaps:** paste `scripts/overlaps.js` into the page and run `btsOverlaps({ overlay: '[data-poster] svg', subject: '[data-poster] [inert] > *, [data-poster] [data-subject-root]' })` for every moment at 1280×800, 1000×760 and 1030×1044. The subject is the component's own root, not the figure round it, or every label counts as on it. It must return nothing. Fix the placement rule, not the one label.
- **Fit:** no page scroll at those sizes, and a resize only changes the scale.
- **Moments:** pick each one. The component, the notes and the curve all follow, and the console stays clean.
- **One value pinned to the source,** such as the poster's duration against the stylesheet.
- **Reduced motion:** the poster tells the truth (no moments row if nothing moves). Check the claim in the specification with reduced motion on: an app-wide rule can override a library's own transitions.
- **Hidden tabs:** an embedded or background preview may not run rAF. Check `document.hidden`, and use headless Playwright for screenshots.

**Done when** every check passes. Say which ones you couldn't run.

## The kit

`assets/kit/` is a React and CSS-modules implementation of everything above. Copy it into the project (`app/specs/kit/` in Next.js, or `src/specs/kit/`) and build each poster as a page beside it. `assets/example/` is a finished poster of a copy button: start from it.

- **`spec-kit.tsx`:**
  - **`SpecPage`:** the poster. Props:
    - `accent`, `name` and `label`;
    - `drawing` (figure 1), `moments`, `notes`, `spec` rows, `fig2` and `units`;
    - `ready`, `error` and `onRetry`;
    - `theme`.
  - **`useTransitionSpec({ fractions, setup })`:** the driver for CSS transitions. `setup(root)` returns:
    - `base` (values at rest);
    - `easing`;
    - `trigger` (the component's own handler);
    - `read` (what to read while it runs);
    - optionally `pick`, to choose among the animations.

    It returns:
    - `m`: the held values, with `elapsed`, `duration`, `easing` and `reduced`;
    - `snapshots`, `selected` and `select`;
    - `ready`, `error` and `retry`;
    - `root`: the ref for the component's wrapper.
  - **Drawing:**
    - `Overlay`;
    - `Dim` and `VDim` (dimensions);
    - `Callout`;
    - `markClass` (line types and hatches);
    - `useCrisp` (hairlines snapped to device pixels);
    - `useDrawingScale`, and `useScreenScale` for a component that has to sit at screen scale 1.
  - **Figures:**
    - `Curve`;
    - `Timeline`;
    - `Moments` (with `crop`, to show just the part that changes).
  - **Reading:**
    - `firstEasing`, `easeAt` and `easeWords`;
    - `stopsOf`, `sampleStops` and `scaleOf` (keyframes: a loop uses one cycle);
    - `within` (box measures to 0.1px);
    - `U` and `Ut` (a number with a lighter unit).
- **`source-kit.ts`:**
  - `useDataState`: drive a component that keeps its state in a data attribute;
  - `startWithout`: put it at its start with no transition;
  - `ms`: parse CSS times.
- **`sheet-states.tsx`:** snapshot capture and the moments row; `oneCamera` (in `spec-kit.tsx`) puts moments captured one at a time in one frame.
- **`sheet-playback.tsx`:** play, pause and slow playback, for posters that offer it.

For scroll, gestures, pointer paths or a JS animation library, write a small driver with the same shape as `useTransitionSpec` that seeks the library's own clock: see [references/drivers.md](references/drivers.md). Outside React, port the layout and conventions; the kit is a reference, not a dependency.

## Deliver

Give the poster's URL, a screenshot of it at 1280×800, and the headline. Then list:
- what was measured;
- anything marked as an estimate;
- any check you couldn't run.

Ensure your app has a theme provider set up: ```tsx // layout.tsx import { ThemeProvider } from "next-themes"; export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return ( {children} ); } ``` --- ## Troubleshooting ### "Unknown registry @reactbits-starter" The `registries` block is missing from `components.json`. Add it per Step 3 above. ### "Unauthorized - License key required" The `REACTBITS_LICENSE_KEY` environment variable is not set. Add it to `.env.local`. ### "Forbidden - Insufficient tier" The user's license tier doesn't include access to the requested content. Starter licenses cannot access `@reactbits-pro` blocks — a Pro or Ultimate license is required. ### Component not found - For components: ensure you're using the `-tw` or `-css` suffix (e.g., `silk-waves-tw`, not `silk-waves`) - For blocks: do NOT add a suffix (e.g., `hero-1`, not `hero-1-tw`) ### Missing `cn` function Install the utility: `npm install clsx tailwind-merge`, then create `lib/utils.ts` with the `cn` function shown in Step 1. ### WebGL/Three.js components show blank - Ensure `three` is installed: `npm install three` - These components require a browser with WebGL support - The component's container must have explicit dimensions (width/height) - For SSR frameworks, the `"use client"` directive handles client-only rendering ### GSAP scroll animations not working - Ensure `gsap` and `@gsap/react` are installed - `ScrollTrigger` is registered automatically in component code - The scroll container must be the default document scroll (not a custom scroll container) unless configured ### Blocks look unstyled - Ensure Tailwind CSS is properly configured - Blocks use Tailwind v4 syntax — if using v3, minor class adjustments may be needed - Check that `globals.css` imports Tailwind: `@import "tailwindcss"` --- ## Best practices 1. **Choose one variant and be consistent** — pick either `-tw` or `-css` for all components in a project 2. **Always use the Tailwind variant (`-tw`) if the project uses Tailwind CSS** — it integrates better and is smaller 3. **Give WebGL components explicit dimensions** — wrap them in a container with set width/height 4. **Lazy-load heavy components** — use `next/dynamic` for Three.js-based components if not above the fold: ```tsx import dynamic from "next/dynamic"; const SilkWaves = dynamic(() => import("@/components/react-bits/silk-waves"), { ssr: false }); ``` 5. **Keep license keys secure** — never hardcode them; always use environment variables 6. **Customize blocks by editing source** — blocks are meant to be starting points, not rigid templates 7. **Preview before installing** — use `npx shadcn@latest view @reactbits-starter/silk-waves-tw` to inspect a component before adding it 8. **Install this skill into projects** — run `npx shadcn@latest add @reactbits-starter/skill` to drop this SKILL.md into the project root so agents always have it available locally

# Global UI/UX Architect & Full Agent QA Skill (`ui-ux-qa` + `cursor/plugins/pstack`)

Never declare a web or native UI/UX task done from `tsc`, `swift build`, or static code inspection alone. Always execute the **6-Loop UI/UX Workflow**, the **13-Point Agent Full QA Monitoring Checklist**, and the **`cursor/plugins/pstack` Verification System** against the live running application with real screenshots, explicit statecharts, Playwright interaction videos (`.webm`) or `orca computer` native captures, and automated geometry checks.

## 1. The 6 Core UI/UX Workflow Loops

Whenever working on UI/UX, execute these 6 loops in order:

1. **Ask questions upfront to validate the idea (`interrogate`)**: Grill the design on edge cases, empty/loading/error/offline states, keyboard navigation, and user roles before locking in the layout.
2. **Create 2 to 3 variants of key UI pieces (`arena`)**: Build side-by-side interactive options (such as compact vs. split vs. inline drawer layouts) so the user can test and compare them live.
3. **Model state machines across scenarios (`statechart`)**: Explicitly model and test `idle`, `loading`, `streaming`, `success`, `empty`, `error`, `offline`, and role/permission transitions using `stateDiagram-v2`.
4. **Try and break what you built (`prove-it-works`)**: Actively red-team the live UI with rapid double-clicks, mid-flight cancels, network errors, keyboard-only navigation, mobile/desktop viewports, and filling every field with the longest realistic value.
5. **Make before/after screenshots when finished (`visual-parity`)**: Capture deterministic Before and After screenshots at matching viewports across Light and Dark themes, and record a Playwright `.webm` interaction video for web PRs.
6. **Setup continuous quality-bar monitoring loops (`poteto-mode` & `hillclimb`)**: Run automated DOM/SwiftUI geometry, WCAG 4.5:1 contrast, and state-machine verification scripts in a loop on every change.

## 2. Full `cursor/plugins/pstack` Knowledge Base (`https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack`)

`pstack` is a composable system of **23 playbooks**, **34 skills**, and **24 engineering principles** built around one core premise: **agent autonomy scales with verification quality**. An agent with a programmatic verification lever (`poteto-mode`) can iterate and self-correct until the UI is genuinely solid, whereas an agent with only a compiler check stops at "it builds" and hands broken layouts to a human.

### A. The 23 `pstack` Playbooks (When to Activate)

1. **`investigation`**: Understand how a component, layout pass, or state coordinator works before writing code.
2. **`bug-fix`**: Diagnose, reproduce (`Before`), surgically fix, and re-verify (`After`) a broken behavior.
3. **`perf`**: Make a hot path, scroll view, or editor interaction measurably faster with baseline and post-change numbers.
4. **`hillclimb`**: Optimize a measurable metric (FPS, CLS, bundle size, layout pass time, contrast pass rate) across iterations.
5. **`runtime-forensics`**: Diagnose live apps that hang, re-enter layout synchronously, leak memory, or swallow errors.
6. **`trace-forensics`**: Analyze profile traces (`.cpuprofile`, Chrome trace JSON, Instruments, `PerformanceObserver`) to locate frame drops or layout thrashing.
7. **`feature`**: Build a new capability end to end with statechart modeling, UI variants, and automated verification.
8. **`refactoring`**: Restructure UI components without changing external behavior, guarded by geometry and snapshot loops.
9. **`prototype`**: Validate whether a layout idea works by building 2 to 3 interactive variants (`arena`).
10. **`visual-parity`**: Match a reference design or verify deterministic Before/After visual improvements across viewports and themes.
11. **`authoring-a-skill`**: Turn recurring debugging or verification workflows into reusable agent skills.
12. **`eval`**: Build a benchmark suite to measure UI quality and catch layout or accessibility regressions across commits.
13. **`babysit`**: Monitor a long-running CI pipeline, macOS JIT runner, or deployment until every check is green.
14. **`shipping`**: Land changes safely and verify health checks, live routes, and tracker tickets.
15. **`autonomous-run`**: Run an unattended multi-step verification loop against a target quality bar.
16. **`orchestrate`**: Coordinate multiple parallel workers or subagents across isolated tasks.
17. **`autopilot-full`**: Full-ceremony lifecycle from requirements interrogation through statechart design, implementation, and QA video/screenshot capture.
18. **`autopilot-stack`**: Stacked PR workflow for multi-layered architecture and UI changes.
19. **`session-pickup`**: Resume an in-progress branch or investigation without losing verification context.
20. **`pause-safely`**: Checkpoint state, artifacts, and open questions cleanly before pausing work.
21. **`multi-phase-plan`**: Decompose complex UI overhauls into gated milestones with explicit verification levers at each gate.
22. **`worktree-cleanup`**: Reconcile and clean up temporary branches and test artifacts after shipping.
23. **`opening-a-pr`**: Package the diff with deterministic Before/After screenshots, statecharts, and a recorded Playwright `.webm` interaction video (or native `orca computer` capture).

### B. The 34 `pstack` Skills (Operational Levers)

- **Core Verification Loop**:
  1. `poteto-mode`: Always-on verification loop (`implement -> launch app/browser -> trigger state -> inspect geometry & screenshot -> break test -> fix`).
  2. `create-verification-skill`: Build the programmatic verification harness and debug overlay (`?debug=1` or `PRYDEA_QA_DEBUG=1`) first so every change is testable in one command.
  3. `maintain-verification-skill`: Keep the verification script synced as new surfaces, roles, and states are added.
  4. `create-formal-verification-skill`: Encode invariants (bounding-box containment, contrast floors, state transitions, accessibility identifiers) as executable assertions.
  5. `benchmark-checklist`: Audit frame timing, node count, layout shift (`CLS = 0`), and render latency.
- **Discovery, Design & State Modeling**:
  6. `interrogate`: Attack the premise and grill the design with high-leverage edge-case questions before locking in layouts.
  7. `statechart`: Model every UI flow as an explicit `stateDiagram-v2` covering all roles, states, error recoveries, and stress inputs.
  8. `arena`: Build 2 to 3 distinct interactive variants of a UI component so the user can compare ergonomics live.
  9. `architect`: Define clean boundaries between presentation, state coordinators, and backend/runtime verification.
  10. `blast-radius`: Trace every surface, test suite, and downstream consumer affected by a UI or token change.
  11. `tdd`: Write failing layout and workflow reproduction tests before applying the surgical fix.
- **Forensics, Quality & Communication**:
  12. `swarm`: Fan out parallel checks across surfaces, viewports, text scales, and themes.
  13. `unslop`: Strip decorative bloat, redundant nested borders, and inconsistent font sizes; keep typography, spacing, and tabular numerals (`tabular-nums`) crisp.
  14. `technical-writing`: Present clear evidence tables, Mermaid statecharts, component evolution timelines, and clickable file links.
  15. **Specialized QA Levers (15 to 34)**: `trace-analysis`, `heap-snapshot`, `dom-geometry-audit`, `touch-target-inspector`, `longest-value-stress`, `pr-video-recorder`, `session-boundary-check`, `ux-research-grounding`, `component-evolution-diff`, `a11y-keyboard-loop`, `network-fault-injection`, `race-condition-breaker`, `reentrancy-guard`, `theme-token-audit`, `contrast-floor-check`, `responsive-split-check`, `ci-gate-runner`, `changeset-audit`, `post-ship-monitor`, `knowledge-sync`.

### C. The 24 `pstack` Principles (Non-Negotiable Engineering Laws)

1. **`prove-it-works`**: "It compiles" is not verification. Observe the change working in the real browser or native app window.
2. **`attack-the-premise`**: Question whether a modal, redundant border, or extra click is needed at all (prefer inline editing and direct manipulation).
3. **`exhaust-the-design-space`**: Explore 2 to 3 UI variants (`arena`) rather than settling on the first layout.
4. **`build-the-lever`**: Invest upfront in a `?debug=1` / `PRYDEA_QA_DEBUG=1` inspector and automated layout test so every iteration verifies in seconds.
5. **`explain-the-number`**: Every performance or geometry claim must cite exact numbers (`0px` overflow, `>= 28pt` desktop / `>= 40px` touch target, WCAG `>= 4.5:1` contrast, `CLS = 0.000`).
6. **`encode-lessons-in-structure`**: Turn every visual or reentrancy bug caught during QA into a permanent automated regression test.
7. **`fail-closed-at-every-boundary`**: Validate inputs, state transitions, and permissions at both the UI layer and the service/runtime boundary.
8. **`make-invisible-states-visible`**: Under a debug flag (`?debug=1` on web or `PRYDEA_QA_DEBUG=1` on native macOS), draw touch targets, split/gesture thresholds, and state transitions directly on screen.
9. **`test-the-longest-realistic-value`**: Fill every input, title, badge, tag bar, and table cell with maximum realistic payloads (`120-char` title, `80-char` branch slug, `66-char` hex address, `12+` tags, wide code lines) and assert zero horizontal overflow or clipping.
10. **`debounce-and-lock-mid-flight`**: Disable or guard primary actions while async saves or worktree realizations are in flight to prevent double-submits.
11. **`ground-in-hci-research`**: Consult established UX discussions and standards (`ux.stackexchange.com`, WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, Apple HIG, Nielsen Norman Group) for typography hierarchy, progressive disclosure, inline vs. modal editing, and truncation rules.
12. **`visualize-iteration-deltas`**: Show how a UI component changed across iterations (`v1 -> v2 -> v3 -> v4`) so design tradeoffs and improvements are transparent.
13. **`record-proof-for-reviewers`**: For web UI/UX PRs, run Playwright with `recordVideo` enabled (`.webm`) and attach the interaction recording to the PR; for native macOS PRs, capture live `orca computer` / 2x Retina before-and-after snapshots.
14. **`zero-silent-swallowing`**: Surface errors inline with actionable retry controls instead of silently dropping failed requests.
15. **`guard-synchronous-layout-reentrancy`**: Never allow synchronous layout flushes (`layoutSubtreeIfNeeded`) inside lazy session or view-map constructors to overwrite re-entrantly mounted state.
16. **`preserve-user-draft-momentum`**: Keep unsaved draft titles, markdown bodies, and filter queries intact across tab switches (`Preview | Source | Split`).
17. **`clean-environment-baseline`**: Reset stale UserDefaults or local storage overrides before visual QA so theme tokens render deterministically.
18. **`keep-hit-targets-humane`**: Interactive controls must maintain `>= 28pt` (`32pt` standard) hit height on desktop and `>= 40px` (`44px` primary CTA) on web/mobile with clear focus rings.
19. **`tabular-numerals-for-telemetry`**: Always apply `monospacedDigit()` / `font-mono tabular-nums` to line numbers, counts, timestamps, and geometry metrics.
20. **`deterministic-state-triggers`**: Expose environment flags or query parameters (`?debug=1`, `PRYDEA_QA_DEBUG=1`) so every state and debug overlay can be triggered deterministically.
21. **`verify-before-and-after`**: Capture matching viewport screenshots before and after every visual or state-machine change.
22. **`minimal-surgical-diff`**: Fix root causes cleanly without introducing speculative abstractions or unrelated churn.
23. **`all-green-ci-gate`**: Never merge a PR until 100% of CI checks and real E2E suites pass.
24. **`compound-agent-knowledge`**: Continually fold newly discovered edge cases back into `SKILL.md` so future runs start smarter.

## 3. The 13-Point Agent Full QA Monitoring Checklist

Execute all 13 checks on every UI/UX task and report the evidence table:

1. **Try and break the stuff built (`prove-it-works`)**: Rapid double-clicks, mid-flight cancel/discard, empty/whitespace-only submissions, narrowest window width (`480pt` stage / `375px` mobile), largest text scale, and synchronous layout reentrancy.
2. **Create state machines (`statechart`) to check different scenarios**: Model and test `empty`, `loading`, `newDraft`, `editing`, `saving`, `realizingWorktree`, `error`, `archived`, and role/permission states using `stateDiagram-v2`.
3. **Make Before/After screenshots when finished (`visual-parity`)**: Capture deterministic side-by-side Before and After screenshots at matching viewports.
4. **Ask pointed questions (`interrogate`) to validate the idea**: Surface overlooked edge cases (such as inline vs. modal creation, gutter rule double-borders, or heading typography scale in markdown summaries) before locking in the design.
5. **Create 2 to 3 variants of a UI piece (`arena`)**: Present concrete variants (for example, `Variant A: Modal Sheet`, `Variant B: Stacked 2-Row Toolbar`, `Variant C: Single-Row Inline Document Header + Unified Tab/Format Strip`) and verify the chosen winner.
6. **Setup loops to maintain a quality bar by constantly monitoring (`poteto-mode`)**: Run automated geometry, contrast, and accessibility identifier checks on every edit.
7. **Draw invisible things under a debug flag (`?debug=1` or `PRYDEA_QA_DEBUG=1`)**: Render touch/hit target bounding badges (`WxH`), split-pane gesture thresholds, and active state transition indicators directly in the UI under the debug flag.
8. **Consult research and discussions from `ux.stackexchange.com`, WAI-ARIA, and Apple HIG**: Ground decisions on line-number gutter contrast, readable markdown body measure (`13pt` body vs. `14pt–17pt` headings), and inline vs. modal cognitive load.
9. **Visualize how a UI component changed across iterations**: Document the component evolution timeline (`v1 -> v2 -> v3 -> v4`) with concrete visual and structural deltas.
10. **Setup loops to profile and fix UI performance (`perf` / `hillclimb`)**: Verify Release-mode build performance, idle CPU (`< 5%`), zero redundant layout passes, and instant tab switching (`Preview | Source | Split`).
11. **Debate edge cases when users interact with the interface**: Explicitly test and resolve conflicts such as switching `Preview -> Source` while composing an untitled draft, filtering while a draft is open, or handling long unbroken markdown lines.
12. **Record Playwright `.webm` interaction video (Web) or live `orca computer` capture (macOS) for GitHub PRs**: Attach recorded visual proof of the interactive verification flow to the PR.
13. **Check when filling every field with the longest realistic value**: Populate every text field, title, slug, tag list, branch input, and markdown body with maximum realistic values and assert zero horizontal overflow (`maxX <= stageWidth`) and zero text clipping.

## 4. `pstack` Web3, 3D WebGL Chassis & Real-Time 60fps Canvas Physics Verification Rules

When building or auditing Web3 consoles, 3D Three.js hardware shells, and real-time 2D/3D canvas games (such as DOPAMINT on NEAR Intents), enforce these additional `pstack` invariants:

1. **Zero Competing Bidirectional `useEffect` Sync Loops (`statechart`)**:
   * Never pair `useEffect([externalProp])` and `useEffect([internalState, onPropChange])` when the parent passes inline callbacks (`onPropChange={(v) => ...}`). An inline callback re-triggers Effect 2 in the same commit as Effect 1, causing external chapter or tab switches to immediately bounce back to the child's stale internal state.
   * Instead, sync `externalProp -> internalState` in one `useEffect([externalProp])` and call `onPropChange(nextVal)` only inside explicit user action handlers (`selectDeviceMode(nextVal)`).
2. **Decouple Action Impulse Sequences from Score Counters (`runtime-forensics`)**:
   * Never trigger physics impulses (such as a bird flap or ball launch) by watching a score counter (`flappyScore !== lastScore`). Scoring a gate, picking up a coin, or resetting score on crash (`setFlappyScore(0)`) will fire a phantom upward impulse and resurrect the entity mid-crash.
   * Always use a dedicated monotonic sequence counter (`flapImpulseSeq`) incremented exclusively by manual flap/jump inputs.
3. **Lock 3D Hardware Overlay Screen Projection During Passive Pointer Movement (`visual-parity`)**:
   * Never tilt a 3D console chassis or recalculate CSS `perspective(...) rotateX(...) rotateY(...)` on the inner HTML screen overlay during passive `pointermove`. Tilt only on explicit pointer drag of the outer bezel and round projected screen coordinates (`Math.round`) so inner controls and charts remain rock-solid (`CLS = 0.000`).
4. **Proportional Canvas Obstacle Geometry & Smooth Axis Auto-Scaling (`prove-it-works`)**:
   * Enforce minimum top and bottom obstacle heights (`>= 14%` of plot height) so top and bottom gates are visually balanced across both compact 3D screens and tall mobile viewports (`392x816`, `390x844`).
   * Exponentially smooth Y-axis `scaleMin` and `scaleMax` (`alpha = 0.14`) so live oracle ticks never cause vertical chart jumping.
   * Suppress start/countdown modal overlays whenever an async settlement (`isSolving`) is in flight.
5. **Canvas & DOM `?debug=1` Telemetry Overlay (`make-invisible-states-visible`)**:
   * Under `?debug=1` (or the live `QA Debug` toggle), render both DOM button hitbox outlines and canvas-level collision circles, AABB obstacle boxes, and AI lookahead trajectory rays, plus a 1-click `Stress Long Values` trigger (`64-char` NEAR account IDs and `66-char` hashes).

## 5. `pstack` Anti-Crowding, Progressive Disclosure & Scannable Microcopy Rules (`unslop` + `ux.stackexchange.com`)

When designing or refactoring authentication gates, multi-step drawers, and Web3 trading terminals (where users must understand the context immediately while reading minimal text):

1. **Short 2-to-3-Word Step Titles & Zero Badge Collisions (`dom-geometry-audit`)**:
   * Never place verbose 30-to-45-character titles (such as `"Enter SNIPER_ACCESS_PASSWORD & Open Terminal"`) inside a flex header row next to a status pill (`[ENTER PASSWORD]`). Long titles wrap onto two lines and collide with the right-hand badge on mobile and `max-w-xl` cards.
   * Use crisp 2-to-3-word titles (`1. Connect Wallet`, `2. Verify Signature`, `3. Access Code`) with `min-w-0 truncate` on the title container and `shrink-0` on the status badge, maintaining `>= 12px` (`gap-3`) separation.
2. **Zero Helper Paragraphs on Locked or Completed Steps (`ground-in-hci-research`)**:
   * Do not render 3-to-4-line explanatory paragraphs telling the user what to do in other steps (`"Complete Step 1 and Step 2 first to unlock Step 3..."`). When a step is locked or already verified, the dimmed border and status pill (`Locked` / `✓ Verified` / `✓ Unlocked`) communicate the state with zero prose clutter.
   * On the active step, show at most 1 concise helper line (`<= 60 chars`).
3. **Never Wrap Raw 66-Character Hex Strings Across Multiple Lines (`unslop`)**:
   * Never dump raw `66-char` object IDs (`0x8832b9f823ea644bda30ec870052303a76b0f12cae85d672fe769247c7e4158f`) or raw wallet addresses as multi-line body text inside form cards.
   * Format on-chain identifiers as single-line truncated monospace pills (`0x0100…bdfd`, `Cap 0x8832…158f`) with `tabular-nums` and a copy button or tooltip for the full value.
4. **Progressive Disclosure for Secondary Overrides & Waitlist Forms (`attack-the-premise`)**:
   * Eliminate "box-in-box-in-box" nested borders (`max 1 card container per step`).
   * Hide secondary or override inputs (such as overriding a default dev wallet address, submitting a new waitlist address, or viewing 30-line PTB/MCP config snippets) behind a 1-click toggle link (`"Custom address"`, `"Join waitlist →"`, `".mcp.json Config"`), and auto-expand them during `S7_LONGEST_VALUE_STRESS` so automated DOM geometry checks still verify `0px` horizontal overflow across every field.

## 6. Embedding Visual Proof in Pull Requests (`opening-a-pr`)

Never list local file paths alone when opening or updating a pull request that touches web or native UI. Reviewers must be able to view deterministic Before/After screenshots and the recorded browser interaction flow directly inside the GitHub PR description without downloading files or bloating the target branch with committed binaries:

1. **Standard Visual Artifact Set (Required for Every UI/UX Feature & Fix)**:
   * Capture `before-desktop.png` and `after-desktop.png` at matching desktop viewports (`1280x800`).
   * Capture `before-mobile.png` and `after-mobile.png` at matching mobile viewports (`390x844`).
   * Record `after-flow.webm` via Playwright `recordVideo` covering the end-to-end interactive flow.
   * For brand-new UI/UX features where the component did not previously exist, capture the baseline page, parent container, or route state on the target base branch as `before-desktop.png` and `before-mobile.png` alongside the new feature state (`after-desktop.png`, `after-mobile.png`, `after-flow.webm`). Never skip `## Visual Proof` on net-new UI features.
2. **Upload & Generate Embeddable PR Markdown (`upload-pr-visual-proof.mjs`)**:
   * Run `node ~/.agents/skills/ui-ux-qa/scripts/upload-pr-visual-proof.mjs --repo <owner/repo> --dir <artifact-dir> --label "<PR summary>"` before calling `gh pr create` or `gh pr edit`.
   * For `PUBLIC` repositories, the script uploads the screenshots, a `ffmpeg` palette-optimized `after-flow.gif` inline preview (because GitHub Markdown sanitizes external `<video>` tags), and the full `after-flow.webm` recording to an unlisted GitHub Gist under the authenticated GitHub account, keeping zero binary commits out of the repository.
   * For `PRIVATE` or `INTERNAL` repositories, the script refuses unauthenticated Gist uploads and requires `--orphan-branch <branch>` so visual assets stay protected behind repository access controls.
3. **Required `## Visual Proof` PR Layout**:
   * Embed the generated `## Visual Proof` section directly into the PR body with a 2-column `Before | After` table for Desktop (`1280x800`), a compact 2-column `Before | After` table (`width="320"`) for Mobile (`390x844`), the inline `after-flow.gif` preview, and a direct download link to `after-flow.webm`.

---
name: glimm
description: Install, wire, and tune glimm — WebGL color-sweep page transitions — in a web project, with correct setup and honest advice about where it fits. Use whenever the user wants page transitions, route-change animations, navigation that feels more alive or polished, mentions glimm by name, or asks for "view transitions with some color" in a Next.js or React site, even if they never name a library. Also use when customizing an existing glimm install — changing palettes, matching brand colors, adjusting sweep timing or direction, or opting specific links out. Also use when a single in-app moment should get a sweep, such as a plan upgrade, a payment landing, a mode change or a generated result.
---

# glimm — color-sweep page transitions

glimm plays a band of WebGL color across the viewport during navigation: the
outgoing page stays ahead of the band, the incoming page is revealed behind it
(a masked page transition). Framework-agnostic
core with React and Next.js adapters. Zero runtime dependencies, MIT.

This skill works with any glimm version. Before writing code, check which
version the project resolves (`npm ls glimm`, or the installed
`node_modules/glimm/package.json`) and treat the installed package as the
source of truth: confirm each export you use exists in its type definitions
(`node_modules/glimm/dist/*.d.ts`). If an API below is missing or named
differently there, follow the installed version and its changelog on
https://glimm.dev/changelog rather than the recipe. On a fresh install, prefer
`npm install glimm@latest`.

The page drawing in towards the action, the page bending with the band, and the
timing that follows a running request all come from `GlimmScope`, added in glimm
0.4. If the installed types don't have it, tell the user that upgrading with
`npm install glimm@latest` brings it. Don't rebuild these effects with custom
shaders.

## Scope: implement glimm and nothing else

Only add and wire glimm. Everything else about the project belongs to its owner,
including copy, error messages, loading designs, layout, styling and app logic.
Unless the user asked for it, don't write or rewrite any of it, and don't add
features around the sweep. If something nearby looks wrong, mention it in a
sentence and leave it as it is.

## Step 1 — Fit check (before touching code)

glimm is a statement, not a default. A sweep takes about a second of the
user's attention on every navigation, so it earns its place on sites where
each navigation is a meaningful scene change — and wears out its welcome
where navigation is a high-frequency tool. Look at the project first
(framework, router, what kind of site it is) and give an honest verdict:

**Good fits:** marketing sites, portfolios, personal sites, blogs and
long-form reading, product launch pages, docs with chaptered reading,
galleries — anywhere a visitor navigates a handful of times per session and
brand personality matters.

**Poor fits:** admin dashboards, data tables, settings panels, multi-step
forms mid-flow, search-and-filter UIs, anything a person navigates dozens of
times an hour. A 1.1 s sweep on every sidebar click becomes friction by the
third click.

If the project is a poor fit, say so plainly and recommend against installing
— that honesty is what makes a "yes" trustworthy. If the user wants it
anyway, respect that, but scope it: shorter timing (`sweepMs: 650`,
`outroMs: 150`), and sweep only major section changes while opting
high-frequency links out with `data-glimm-skip` (Step 4).

That verdict is about sweeping navigation. A product that is a poor fit for
sweeps on every link can still earn one on a single moment, as long as it
happens rarely and changes something the person cares about. In that case skip
`InterceptLinks` and use the in-app recipe in Step 2.

Accessibility and robustness are not reasons to hesitate: glimm respects
`prefers-reduced-motion` (navigates instantly) and degrades to plain
navigation when WebGL is unavailable. Both are automatic — never write your
own reduced-motion guard around it.

## Step 2 — Install and wire

```bash
npm install glimm
```

`react` and `next` are optional peer dependencies — nothing else is pulled in.

### Next.js App Router (the common case)

Mount once in the **root layout**, wrapping the body content:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import { GlimmProvider, InterceptLinks } from 'glimm/next'

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <GlimmProvider palette="prism">
          <InterceptLinks />
          {children}
        </GlimmProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

That is the whole install. `<InterceptLinks />` runs every internal link
click through a sweep automatically — plain `<a>` and `next/link` both work
unchanged, and it already leaves alone: modifier-clicks, middle-clicks,
`target="_blank"`, downloads, external origins, and same-page hash links.
Don't re-implement any of those guards.

Wiring rules that matter, and why:

- **Root layout, not a nested one.** A provider in a nested layout remounts
  when the user navigates across layout boundaries, killing the shader
  context mid-flight and dropping the transition.
- **One entry point per app.** Import everything from `glimm/next` (or, in a
  non-Next app, everything from `glimm/react`). Mixing entry points creates
  two React contexts, and `useGlimm()` from one can't see the provider from
  the other.
- **The root layout can stay a server component.** `GlimmProvider` and
  `InterceptLinks` are client components already; importing them does not
  require `'use client'` in the layout file.

### Per-navigation control (optional, add only where needed)

```tsx
'use client'
import { TransitionLink, useTransitionRouter } from 'glimm/next'

// Declarative — a drop-in next/link replacement:
<TransitionLink href="/work" sweep={{ palette: 'berry', direction: 'rtl' }}>
  Work
</TransitionLink>

// Programmatic — for form submits / post-action redirects:
const router = useTransitionRouter()
await save(form)
router.push('/done', { palette: 'ember' })
```

`TransitionLink` and `InterceptLinks` coexist safely — the link's own handler
takes the click and the interceptor sees it as already handled, so nothing
double-fires.

### In-app moments

A sweep doesn't need a route change. It can mark a state change on the current
page, which is often the better use of it inside a product. There are two ways
to do it, and `GlimmScope` is the better one wherever the installed version has it:

- **`GlimmScope`** wraps one box, which can be a page, a section or a card. It
  takes the app's real work, keeps the change behind the band, and moves the
  content under the band where the browser can. See the next section.
- **`sweep()`** from `useGlimm` covers the viewport and needs no change to the
  page's structure. It's the choice for a version without `GlimmScope`, or when
  the user only wants the band.

```tsx
'use client'
import { useGlimm } from 'glimm/next'  // or 'glimm/react' outside Next

const { sweep } = useGlimm()
sweep(() => setPlan('pro'), { sweepMs: 800 })
```

A moment earns a sweep when it is rare and the person would want to notice it:
a plan upgrade, a payment landing, a mode they switched on, a result they waited
for, a teammate joining. Routine actions don't earn one, including saves, row
edits, checkbox ticks and anything repeated many times in a session. An event
nobody pressed for, such as a payment arriving, sweeps the same way, called from
wherever the event is handled. Keep `sweep()` moments shorter than a navigation,
at around 650 to 900 ms.

### Moving the page with `GlimmScope`

```tsx
'use client'
import { useRef, useState } from 'react'
import { GlimmScope, type GlimmScopeHandle } from 'glimm/next' // or 'glimm/react'

const scope = useRef<GlimmScopeHandle>(null)

const upgrade = (event: React.MouseEvent) => {
  const r = event.currentTarget.getBoundingClientRect()
  setBusy(true) // answers the press, outside the scope's timing
  scope.current?.play({
    at: [r.left + r.width / 2, r.top + r.height / 2], // the page leans in towards the button
    work: async () => {
      const res = await fetch('/api/upgrade', { method: 'POST' })
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Upgrade failed') // a rejection means no sweep
    },
    change: () => setPlan('pro'),  // runs as soon as the work is done, behind the band
    onBurst: () => setBusy(false), // the band has broken away
    onFail: () => setBusy(false),  // no sweep, and the page stays as it was
  })
}

<GlimmScope ref={scope} curve={0.12} direction="ttb" sweepMs={2700} style={{ position: 'absolute', inset: 0 }}>
  <Billing />
</GlimmScope>
```

It doesn't need `GlimmProvider`, so a project that only wants one moment can use
it alone. The rules for using it:

- **Don't check for browser support.** Where HTML-in-Canvas is available, the
  content breathes in towards the action and ripples as the band passes.
  Everywhere else it's a plain sweep over the same box with the change still behind
  the band. Reduced motion is handled too, so never write a guard or a second code
  path, and never hold a feature back for a browser version. This is why it's
  safe to use without asking.
- **`work` holds the real work, and `change` holds the result.** Both go in
  `play()`, so don't await the request first as you would with `sweep()`. The work
  starts on the press, the page leans in while it runs, and however long it takes
  the movement stays one breath. `change` receives the work's result. Make `work`
  reject on failure, including a bad response status, since `fetch` doesn't throw
  on a 500.
- **The pressed control's busy state stays outside.** Set it before `play()`, clear
  it in `onBurst` and `onFail`, and don't wait for `onLeave`.
- **Pass `anticipate: true` only for what nobody pressed**, such as a payment
  arriving. It gives the page time to lean in fully before the change, which would
  be a wait for anyone who just asked for something. Without `work`, `change` runs
  right on the press.
- **A later `play()` interrupts**, so don't queue plays or disable controls until
  one ends. `play()` also returns `{ fastForward, cancel }`.
- **Give the box a size.** The scope clips to its box and fills it, so size it with
  `style`, and fit it to the layout that's already there. The example's
  `position: 'absolute', inset: 0` suits a view inside a positioned shell, and it
  fills the viewport if there's no positioned ancestor, so don't use it on a page
  in normal flow. In a flex shell, `flex: 1, minHeight: 0` fills the content area.
  A section or card needs a set height, because where the page effect runs, the
  content doesn't give the box its size and it would collapse to nothing. Content
  that scrolls must scroll
  inside the scope, not in the document around it. What renders outside it, such
  as a portalled toast or dialog, doesn't move and isn't covered by the band.
- **Lean in towards the action.** Pass `at` for whatever was pressed, since without
  it the page leans in towards the `origin` prop, which is the top centre by default.
  `at` is measured from the box's top-left in CSS px, so the example works because
  its box starts at the top-left of the viewport. For any other box, subtract the
  box's own position. For an action that never moves, or an event nobody pressed,
  set `origin` as fractions of the box instead, such as `origin={[0.5, 1]}` for a
  composer at the bottom.
- **Let the band take its time across a whole page.** The 650 to 900 ms above is for
  `sweep()`. A scope's band defaults to 1600 ms, and about 2700 ms suits a whole
  page, since the band fades out well before it arrives at the far side.
- **Keep to a handful per page, not one per row.** Each scope uses its own WebGL
  contexts, and a page can only keep 16 alive.

Only add the `usePageEffect()` reader switch if the user asks for a way to turn
the effect off.

### Other setups

For **React without Next** (Vite + react-router, etc.), **Next Pages
Router**, or **vanilla JS / other frameworks**, read
[references/react-and-vanilla.md](references/react-and-vanilla.md) — the
Pages Router in particular must use `glimm/react`, not `glimm/next` (the Next
adapter is built on `next/navigation`, which is App Router only).

### The change goes inside the sweep

A sweep reveals a change, so the visible change must never come before the
band. Put the state update or navigation inside the callback you pass to
`sweep()`, and keep everything it affects inside the swept area. glimm then
runs it while the band is crossing.

```tsx
// Right: the new state appears behind the band
sweep(() => setPublished(true))

// Wrong: the new state is on screen before the band arrives
setPublished(true)
sweep(async () => {})
```

If the result comes from a request, await the request first and call `sweep()`
when it resolves. A loading state on the pressed button can start right away,
since it's feedback for the press. Anything that belongs to the result, such
as a legend, count or badge, changes with the sweep.

### The sweep never makes anyone wait

The animation follows the app, so the app never waits for the animation.

- **Answer the press straight away.** The pressed control shows its loading or
  selected state immediately, outside the sweep. The result goes inside, and that
  includes clearing the loading state, so the old page doesn't flip back to its
  idle look just before the band reveals the new one.
- **Never add a delay.** Don't use `setTimeout`, and don't await `done` or
  `midpoint`, to line a change up with the band or to keep a control busy until
  the sweep ends. `sweep()` applies the change
  itself, and it does so as early as it can while keeping the change hidden.
- **Keep slow work out of the callback.** The band can't start until the callback
  has finished, and the page is held until then. Await the request first so the
  page stays usable, then call `sweep()` with the result. A route change is fine
  to return from the callback, since it is the change being revealed.
- **Only sweep on success.** Check the result before calling `sweep()`, including
  the response status, since `fetch` doesn't throw on a 500. A failed request gets
  no sweep, because the sweep tells the person it worked. What the app does about
  a failure is the project's own decision, so leave that alone.
- **Let a new action interrupt.** A second `sweep()` replaces the one playing, so
  don't queue sweeps or disable controls until one finishes. Where the browser
  supports View Transitions, the page doesn't take clicks while a sweep plays,
  which is another reason to keep in-app sweeps short and rare.

### Size it to what changed, and start from the action

The sweep should be about as big as the change, and it should appear to come
from whatever caused it.

- **The whole page or view changed:** wrap it in a scope with `curve={0.12}`, or
  use the provider's `sweep()`, which covers the viewport.
- **Something notable changed in one place:** use a scope around the page with
  `curve={0.22} span={0.64} fade={[0.16, 0.64]}`, so the band stays near the change
  and is gone by mid-page.
- **One element changed:** put a scope around just that element with `curve={0.06}
  bandTight={34}`. Without `GlimmScope`, use the container recipe below. A
  full-page sweep for a change in one card makes a small moment feel bigger than
  it is.

Pick the `direction` that travels away from the action, so a composer at the bottom
of the screen sweeps `btt` and a control in the top bar sweeps `ttb`. A scope can
also go `ltr`, for an action in a sidebar, or `rtl`.

On phones, primary actions usually sit near the bottom of the screen, so a
`btt` sweep often reads best there even when the desktop layout uses another
direction. Nothing about a sweep may depend on hover, so trigger it from the
action itself and check it with touch.

### Sweeping inside a container

`GlimmScope` already does all of this, so this recipe is for a version without it.
When the sweep plays inside one element rather than the whole page (a card,
a chart, a table), the band must fade out towards that box's edges — never
let it end on a hard border. Versions of glimm with a `feather` option on
`createShader` do this by default. Version 0.3.1 and earlier don't have that
option, so mask the canvas edges in CSS there, after checking the installed
types. This recipe is a decorative sweep only, so make the change in `onMidpoint`
rather than through the provider's masking. The recipe is in
[references/react-and-vanilla.md](references/react-and-vanilla.md#sweeping-inside-a-container).

## Step 3 — Pick a palette with intent

Don't leave the default without looking. Find the project's brand colors
(CSS custom properties, Tailwind config, design tokens) and choose the preset
whose hues live nearest to them:

| Preset   | Hues                        | Reads as |
| -------- | --------------------------- | -------- |
| `spectrum` | one full hue cycle        | every color at once — the default from 0.4 |
| `prism`  | cyan → violet → magenta     | iridescent, techy — the default before 0.4 |
| `berry`  | red-pink → magenta          | warm, bold, editorial |
| `lagoon` | blue → cyan → green         | cool, calm, natural |
| `citrus` | green → yellow → orange     | energetic, playful |
| `azure`  | cyan → blue → violet        | corporate-clean, trustworthy |
| `ember`  | yellow → orange → red-pink  | hot, urgent, dramatic |

For an exact brand match, build a custom palette from the brand's own hexes:

```tsx
import { accentChain } from 'glimm/next'  // also exported from glimm/react and glimm

const brand = accentChain(['#7C3AED', '#EC4899'])  // 2–4 stops, in sweep order
<GlimmProvider palette={brand}>
```

`accentChain` interpolates the stops in OKLCH (perceptually even, no muddy
midpoints) and fits the shader's palette to them. On dark sites, add
`brightness={0.85}` to the provider so the band doesn't bloom against the
dark background. Deeper tuning — timing, easing, direction, band shape, feel
recipes — is in [references/tuning.md](references/tuning.md).

## Step 4 — Curate which links sweep

The sweep should mark *scene changes*, not every click. Walk the project's
nav and opt out anything high-frequency or intra-scene with
`data-glimm-skip`:

- pagination, table sorting, filters
- tab switches within a page
- footer utility links (privacy, terms)
- anything that opens in a modal or drawer rather than a new scene

```tsx
<Link href="/work?page=2" data-glimm-skip>Next page</Link>
```

Primary navigation (header links, cards into detail pages, prominent CTAs)
keeps the sweep. If after curation only two or three links would sweep,
reconsider `InterceptLinks` entirely and use explicit `<TransitionLink>` on
just those — intent-revealing beats blanket-plus-exceptions.

## Step 5 — Verify it works

Never hand back unverified. Start the dev server and click through two or
three real navigations, then check:

1. The sweep plays and the new page appears **behind** the band (no flash of
   unstyled or duplicate content). It's often too fast to judge at full speed,
   so temporarily set `sweepMs` to about 5000 and watch it again. Nothing that
   belongs to the result may be visible before the band reaches it. Put
   `sweepMs` back afterwards.
2. The browser console is clean — no glimm warnings, no WebGL errors.
3. A Cmd/Ctrl-click still opens a new tab with no sweep in the original.
4. External links and hash links behave as before.
5. Browser back/forward behave as the installed version documents — in
   current releases they are instant with no sweep, which is expected, not a
   bug.
6. The pressed control responds immediately, with no pause before anything
   happens, and pressing something else straight after a sweep starts still
   works.
7. It still reads well at phone width, with the direction you chose.
8. For a `GlimmScope`, a failed request plays no sweep and leaves the page as it
   was. If the browser you're checking in has no HTML-in-Canvas, a plain sweep is
   the correct result, not a bug, and the page only moves in one that has it.

If something is off, check Troubleshooting below before changing the wiring.

## Step 6 — Hand back short and natural

Keep the final reply brief and conversational — a few sentences, not a
report. The user just watched a two-file change; don't recite this skill back
at them with headers and checklists. Cover only:

- what changed (usually `package.json` + the root layout) and the install
  command if you couldn't run it,
- the knob or two they'll actually touch (`palette`, `sweepMs` — props on
  `GlimmProvider`),
- the removal path in one line (delete the provider + `InterceptLinks`,
  `npm uninstall glimm`) — reversibility makes it safe to try.

Anything that needs flagging gets a sentence, not a section — "I couldn't run
this offline, so click through a couple of pages after `npm install`" is
enough. If the site is running, offering one alternate preset ("want to see
it in `lagoon`?") beats describing palettes.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause → fix |
| ------- | ----------- |
| `useGlimm must be used inside <GlimmProvider>` | Component imports from a different entry point than the provider, or the provider is in a nested layout. One entry point, root layout. |
| No sweep, instant navigation, no errors | OS has reduced motion enabled, or no WebGL (headless browser, some VMs). This is the designed fallback, not a failure. |
| New content appears, then the band plays over it | The state changed outside the sweep callback. Move the update into `sweep(() => ...)`. |
| The page freezes, then the sweep plays late | Slow work is inside the sweep callback. Await the request first, then call `sweep()` with the result. |
| User asks for the page to bend or draw inwards like the glimm.dev demos | Use `GlimmScope`. If the installed types don't have it, upgrade with `npm install glimm@latest`, and don't build a custom shader. |
| A `GlimmScope` plays a sweep but the page doesn't move | The browser has no HTML-in-Canvas (Chrome 157 and later), which is the designed fallback, or the reader turned it off through `usePageEffect`. |
| Nothing shows inside a `GlimmScope`, or the band runs far past the screen | The box has no useful size. Set its height through `style`, and let content scroll inside it. |
| Sweep plays but the page "jumps" at the end | An old glimm (<0.3.1) without View-Transition masking. `npm install glimm@latest`. |
| Links to other origins sweep weirdly / break | They shouldn't be intercepted at all — check for a custom `shouldIntercept` that dropped the origin check. |
| A sweep inside a card or chart ends on a hard edge | The canvas has `feather: 0`, or glimm predates `feather`. Leave `feather` at `'auto'`, or mask the canvas edges in CSS (see references/react-and-vanilla.md). |
| Band too bright / washed out on dark theme | Set `brightness={0.85}` (or lower) on the provider. |
| TypeScript can't find `glimm/next` | Older `moduleResolution`. Needs `"bundler"` or `"node16"`/`"nodenext"` in tsconfig — glimm ships ESM with `exports` maps only. |
| Dev-only double navigation in React 18 StrictMode (non-Next) | Make sure the navigate callback is idempotent; the provider awaits it once per sweep, but app-level listeners added twice will fire twice. |
